Although an Iranian lower court initially found merit in Masihzadeh's plagiarism claim, a panel of copyright experts at Tehran University later cleared Farhadi of the charges, ruling that real-life historical events cannot be copyrighted.
He served on the main competition jury of the 75th Cannes Film Festival in 2022, alongside actors Rebecca Hall and Deepika Padukone, under the presidency of French actor Vincent Lindon.
Farhadi was named one of Time magazine's 100 most influential people in the world in 2012, with an introductory tribute written by American film critic Richard Corliss.

Before establishing himself as an auteur, he co-wrote the screenplay for Ebrahim Hatamikia's 2002 thriller 'Low Heights', a tense hostage drama about an airplane hijacking that became a major box-office hit in Iran.

He briefly relocated to Paris to shoot his 2013 drama 'The Past' (Le Passé), working with French star Bérénice Bejo, who won the Best Actress award at Cannes for her performance under his meticulous direction.

name: Barry Jenkins
name_meaning: The surname Jenkins is of Flemish and English origin, operating as a patronymic meaning 'kin of Jenk' (a diminutive of John, meaning 'God is gracious'). The given name Barry is an Anglicized form of the Irish name Bairre, a diminutive of Fionnbharr, meaning 'fair-haired' or 'fair-headed'.
intro: Barry Jenkins is an American filmmaker whose lyrical, deeply empathetic cinema explores Black identity, systemic trauma, and the yearning for connection, best exemplified by his historic Best Picture-winning masterpiece Moonlight and his lush adaptation of James Baldwin's work.

facts.text: Born in 1979 in Miami's Liberty City public housing project, Jenkins was raised in a cramped, overcrowded apartment where he often had to sleep on the floor.
He was named after his biological father, who separated from his mother before Jenkins was born, leaving the young boy to believe his father was dead until he learned the truth at age 12.
Due to his mother's severe crack cocaine addiction, Jenkins was legally separated from her at age 12 and raised by an older woman named Minerva, who had previously taken in his older brother.

He played football at Miami Northwestern Senior High School, the exact same school attended by playwright Tarell Alvin McCraney, though the two never crossed paths despite their eerily similar backgrounds.

Jenkins initially enrolled at Florida State University to study English and creative writing, but impulsively switched to the film program after seeing a sign for it outside Doak Campbell Stadium, despite having zero prior filmmaking experience.
At FSU, he was introduced to international cinema for the first time, experiencing a profound artistic awakening through Claire Denis’s Beau Travail and Wong Kar-wai’s Chungking Express.
He met his core lifelong creative collaborators at FSU's film school, including cinematographer James Laxton, producer Adele Romanski, and editors Joi McMillon and Nat Sanders.

During his early post-college days in Los Angeles, he worked as a director's assistant at Oprah Winfrey's Harpo Films but ultimately quit because the corporate environment felt too far removed from actual directing.
He financed his 2008 debut feature, Medicine for Melancholy, with $15,000 borrowed from a friend, Justin Barber, who had received a sudden financial windfall.

Following his debut, Jenkins endured an agonizing eight-year hiatus from feature filmmaking, supporting himself by working as a carpenter and co-founding a commercial production company called Strike Anywhere.
He proved he could still capture striking cinematic imagery during his hiatus by creating the 2011 short film Chlorophyl, shooting it entirely in Miami on a consumer-grade Canon 7D DSLR camera.
He discovered the source material for Moonlight—Tarell Alvin McCraney's unproduced Yale School of Drama play In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue—through the Miami-based Borscht arts collective.
To gain emotional distance from the heavy, deeply personal Miami-based subject matter, Jenkins wrote the screenplay for Moonlight during a six-week European retreat in Brussels, Belgium.

During the filming of Moonlight, he strictly kept the three actors playing the protagonist Chiron (Alex Hibbert, Ashton Sanders, Trevante Rhodes) separated, ensuring they wouldn't subconsciously mimic each other's mannerisms.

He frequently incorporates the 'chopped and screwed' technique of Houston hip-hop into his film scores, working with composer Nicholas Britell to slow down and pitch-shift classical orchestral tracks to create a hazy, subjective auditory experience.

Jenkins's historic 2017 Best Picture Oscar win for Moonlight was infamously announced only after La La Land had been incorrectly declared the winner due to an unprecedented envelope mix-up by PwC accountants.
With Moonlight, Jenkins directed the first film with an all-Black cast, and the first LGBTQ-themed film, to ever win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

He wrote the screenplay adaptation for James Baldwin's If Beale Street Could Talk in 2013 during the same Brussels trip where he wrote Moonlight, long before he actually secured the rights from the famously protective Baldwin estate.

To win over the Baldwin estate, Jenkins sent a heartfelt letter alongside a custom visual lookbook and his unsolicited screenplay, successfully convincing Baldwin's sister, Gloria Karefa-Smart, to grant him the rights.

While directing the Amazon limited series The Underground Railroad in 2021, Jenkins insisted on having an on-set guidance counselor to help the cast and crew process the severe psychological trauma of recreating American slavery.

Jenkins met his romantic partner, acclaimed The Farewell director Lulu Wang, on the film festival circuit, and the two filmmakers now share a workspace where they rigorously critique each other's scripts.

He shocked the indie film world by agreeing to direct Disney's CGI blockbuster prequel Mufasa: The Lion King, a pivot he justified by citing his deep emotional connection to the script's themes of brotherhood and orphanage.
When Jenkins's FSU classmate Joi McMillon was nominated for an Oscar for cutting Moonlight, Jenkins proudly championed her milestone as the first Black woman ever nominated for Best Film Editing.

name: Ben Affleck
name_meaning: Benjamin is derived from the Hebrew 'Binyāmīn' (בִּנְיָמִין), meaning 'son of the right hand,' while his Scottish surname Affleck originates from the Gaelic 'Achadh nan Leac' (field of flat stones). His middle name, Géza, is a traditional Hungarian name given to him by his parents to honor a close family friend who had survived the Holocaust.
intro: Catapulted from Boston indie obscurity to Oscar-winning wunderkind, Ben Affleck weathered severe tabloid overexposure and public struggles with alcoholism to methodically reinvent himself as an acclaimed, gritty director of American crime thrillers and historical dramas.

facts.text: His father, Timothy Affleck, worked as an auto mechanic, a carpenter, a bookie, and famously as a janitor at Harvard University—a job that directly inspired the premise of his breakthrough film, Good Will Hunting.
He spent a year traveling across Mexico at age thirteen while starring in the PBS educational series The Voyage of the Mimi, an experience that left him entirely fluent in Spanish.

Before his Hollywood success, Affleck majored in Middle Eastern affairs at Occidental College in Los Angeles, a brief academic pursuit that later informed his meticulous recreation of the 1979 Iran hostage crisis in Argo.

Affleck honed his acting skills under the strict tutelage of Gerry Speca, the legendary drama teacher at Cambridge Rindge and Latin School, whom both he and Damon publicly thanked during their 1998 Academy Award acceptance speech.

In their early twenties, Affleck, Damon, and Affleck's younger brother Casey lived together in a rented house in Eagle Rock, Los Angeles, where they spent their days writing Good Will Hunting and throwing massive parties.
At twenty-five years old, Affleck became the youngest person in history to win the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay.

Before filming the 1998 blockbuster Armageddon, director Michael Bay and producer Jerry Bruckheimer forced Affleck to undergo $20,000 worth of dental work to cap his uneven teeth so he could convincingly play a heroic leading man.
He is a highly skilled card player who defeated Tobey Maguire and other celebrities to win the 2004 California State Poker Championship, taking home a $356,400 first prize.
In 2014, Affleck was detained by security and permanently banned from playing blackjack at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas after managers caught him counting cards.

For his 2007 directorial debut, Gone Baby Gone, he cast his younger brother Casey Affleck in the lead role and shot extensively in actual Boston dive bars, using real-life local patrons instead of professional extras.

Despite directing Argo to a Best Picture victory at the 2013 Academy Awards, Affleck was shockingly omitted from the Best Director category, making Argo the first film since Driving Miss Daisy to win the top prize without a directing nomination.

Moving away from typical celebrity charities, Affleck founded the Eastern Congo Initiative in 2010, traveling to the Democratic Republic of Congo more than a dozen times to direct grants to local, community-building organizations.

Affleck has been highly public about his own hereditary struggles with alcoholism, completing multiple stints in rehab in 2001, 2017, and 2018, the last of which he was driven to by his ex-wife Jennifer Garner.

During the 2014 Sony email hack, leaked correspondence revealed that Affleck had successfully pressured the PBS genealogical show Finding Your Roots to censor the discovery that one of his maternal ancestors owned slaves in Georgia.

As a lifelong Massachusetts native, Affleck's daily, paparazzi-documented obsession with Dunkin' iced coffee culminated in him directing and starring in a massive 2023 Super Bowl commercial for the brand alongside his wife, Jennifer Lopez.

His high-profile relationship with Jennifer Lopez in the early 2000s resulted in the media coining the term "Bennifer," widely considered the first major portmanteau name of the modern celebrity tabloid era.

While preparing to direct the Boston crime thriller The Town, Affleck interviewed real-life former bank robbers from the Charlestown neighborhood and visited maximum-security prisons to ensure the dialogue and tactics were flawlessly accurate.

The critical and commercial disaster of his 2003 film Gigli deeply depressed Affleck, leading him to essentially quit acting in major blockbusters for several years to reinvent himself as a serious behind-the-camera filmmaker.

In 2003, he purchased a sprawling, 87-acre estate on Hampton Island, Georgia, featuring a mansion built to resemble a Greek Revival Southern plantation, which he later struggled to sell for years amid public discomfort over its antebellum aesthetics.

In 2022, Affleck and Matt Damon founded the independent production company Artists Equity, designed to share profits with the entire crew, and its first film was the Affleck-directed Air about the creation of the Air Jordan shoe.

He is the only actor to have appeared in almost every film of Kevin Smith's "View Askewniverse" franchise, frequently portraying different characters, most notably the comic book artist Holden McNeil in Chasing Amy.

name: Ben Stiller
name_meaning: The name Benjamin comes from the Hebrew בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin), meaning 'son of the right hand' or 'son of the south.' The surname Stiller is a German and Ashkenazi Jewish nickname derived from the Middle High German 'stille,' meaning 'calm,' 'quiet,' or 'silent.'
intro: An American actor, comedian, and filmmaker, Ben Stiller rose to fame through sharp satirical comedies before evolving into an acclaimed, exacting director of prestige television, utilizing his lifelong Hollywood immersion to deconstruct the entertainment industry and modern alienation.

facts.text: At age ten, he began shooting Super 8 movies with his sister Amy, often crafting elaborate cinematic revenge plots against the childhood bullies who picked on him.

While attending the Calhoun School, a teenage Stiller played drums in a post-punk band called Capital Punishment, which released an obscure 1982 album titled 'Roadkill' that was surprisingly reissued by an indie label 36 years later.
He landed a small acting role in Steven Spielberg's 1987 World War II drama 'Empire of the Sun', an experience that profoundly influenced his own visual ambitions as a director.
He directed a short parody of 'The Color of Money' called 'The Hustler of Money', which caught the attention of both Tom Cruise and 'Saturday Night Live' creator Lorne Michaels.

Lorne Michaels hired him as a writer and featured player for 'Saturday Night Live' in 1989, but Stiller abruptly quit after just four episodes because the show refused to let him make pre-taped short films.
He co-created the sketch comedy 'The Ben Stiller Show' for MTV and later Fox, which suffered such low ratings it was canceled before it won the 1993 Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing.
A lifelong 'Star Trek' fanatic, Stiller named his production company Red Hour Productions after the 'Red Hour' riot featured in the original series episode 'The Return of the Archons'.

He directed the dark comedy 'The Cable Guy' (1996), a critical and commercial disappointment at the time that nevertheless made history by securing star Jim Carrey a record-breaking $20 million salary.

Stiller directed the legendary 1999 sci-fi comedy pilot 'Heat Vision and Jack' starring Jack Black as a former astronaut and Owen Wilson as the voice of a talking motorcycle, but Fox executives found it too bizarre and refused to pick it up.
It was while directing the rejected 'Heat Vision and Jack' pilot that Stiller met actress Christine Taylor, whom he married a year later.

His 2001 fashion-industry satire 'Zoolander' was strictly banned by the censorship board of Malaysia because the film's central plot revolves around brainwashing a male model to assassinate the Malaysian Prime Minister.
He frequently cast his parents in his directorial projects, most notably giving his father Jerry the role of eccentric modeling agent Maury Ballstein in 'Zoolander'.

Upon the release of 'Tropic Thunder', Stiller faced intense protests and a boycott from disability advocacy groups over the film's 'Simple Jack' subplot, which he defended as a satire of Oscar-hungry actors rather than a mockery of the disabled.

He convinced Tom Cruise to wear a bald cap and fat suit to play the profane studio executive Les Grossman in 'Tropic Thunder', a character Cruise largely improvised based on his own experiences with Hollywood producers.

In 2014, Stiller was secretly diagnosed with intermediate-risk prostate cancer and underwent a successful surgery to remove his prostate, later crediting the controversial PSA blood test with saving his life.
Stiller holds the Guinness World Record for the longest selfie stick—measuring 8.56 meters—which he commissioned and used to take a photo at the London premiere of 'Zoolander 2' in 2016.

Stiller and Christine Taylor announced their separation in 2017 after 17 years of marriage, but the couple fully reconciled during the COVID-19 pandemic after he moved back into their family home to be with their children during the lockdown.

Shifting away from broad comedy, Stiller directed all seven episodes of the gritty 2018 prison break miniseries 'Escape at Dannemora', utilizing actual locations at the Clinton Correctional Facility in upstate New York.

His pivot to prestige television continued as the primary director and executive producer of the acclaimed dystopian Apple TV+ series 'Severance' (2022), which earned him a Directors Guild of America Award.

Since 2018, Stiller has served as a Goodwill Ambassador for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), traveling to conflict zones in Lebanon, Guatemala, and Ukraine to meet with displaced families.
During a 2022 humanitarian trip to Kyiv amidst the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Stiller met with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy—a fellow former comedy actor—and publicly declared him 'my hero.'
A passionate tennis fan and player, Stiller is a frequent, highly visible presence in the front row at the US Open in Queens and counts professional player Rafael Nadal among his close friends.

name: Bernardo Bertolucci
name_meaning: The given name Bernardo is the Italian form of Bernard, derived from the Germanic elements 'bern' (bear) and 'hard' (brave or hardy), translating to 'brave as a bear.' The surname Bertolucci is a patronymic derived from Bertoluccio, a diminutive of Berto, which stems from the Germanic 'beraht' meaning 'bright' or 'famous.'
intro: A Marxist poet turned cinematic provocateur, Bernardo Bertolucci merged sweeping historical epics with intimate Freudian psychoanalysis. Capturing the ideological turbulence of 20th-century Italy, he weathered obscenity trials to become the sole Italian to win the Best Director Oscar.

facts.text: Raised in the affluent countryside of Parma, Bertolucci was the son of the celebrated Italian poet and film critic Attilio Bertolucci, who regularly hosted local intellectuals at their sprawling estate.
At age fifteen, he borrowed a 16mm camera to shoot his first short films, The Cableway and Death of a Pig, documenting rural life around his family's home in the Apennine mountains.
Before committing to cinema, he followed in his father's literary footsteps, winning Italy's prestigious Premio Viareggio at age twenty-one for his 1962 debut poetry collection, In cerca del mistero.

Bertolucci's entry into filmmaking was the direct result of a literary favor: his father helped publish the debut novel of Pier Paolo Pasolini, and in return, Pasolini hired the twenty-year-old Bernardo—who had zero on-set experience—as the first assistant director for his 1961 film Accattone.
To accept Pasolini's offer, Bertolucci permanently dropped out of the University of Rome, where he had been studying modern literature.

He co-wrote the original story treatment for Sergio Leone's 1968 epic Once Upon a Time in the West alongside Dario Argento, famously convincing Leone to center the narrative around a female protagonist played by Claudia Cardinale.

A devout Marxist who officially joined the Italian Communist Party in 1969, Bertolucci frequently wrestled with the guilt of being an unapologetic bourgeois intellectual making expensive films for a capitalist industry.

He underwent rigorous Freudian psychoanalysis for over a decade, a process that profoundly shaped the doppelgänger motifs and repressed sexual traumas central to his 1970 fascist-era masterpiece, The Conformist.

His idolization of French New Wave pioneer Jean-Luc Godard soured into a bitter feud when Godard, despising The Conformist for its commercial gloss, handed Bertolucci a Maoist pamphlet in silent protest—which the Italian director furiously threw to the ground and stomped on.

During the filming of Last Tango in Paris, Bertolucci and Marlon Brando conspired on the morning of the shoot to use a stick of butter as a lubricant for a simulated rape scene without informing nineteen-year-old actress Maria Schneider, because the director wanted her to react 'as a girl, not as an actress.'

In 1976, Italy's highest court convicted Bertolucci of obscenity for Last Tango in Paris, sentencing him to a suspended prison term, stripping him of his civil voting rights for five years, and ordering all domestic prints of the film to be incinerated.

His 1976 historical epic 1900 became a legendary production nightmare, ballooning to a five-hour-and-seventeen-minute runtime that sparked a vicious, years-long legal battle over final cut with Paramount Pictures and producer Alberto Grimaldi.

He met his second wife, British screenwriter and director Clare Peploe, on the set of 1900, and they remained married for forty years until his death, frequently collaborating on scripts like Besieged.
He was granted unprecedented access by the Chinese government to shoot The Last Emperor inside Beijing's Forbidden City, becoming the first Western filmmaker authorized to do so.

The Last Emperor swept the 1988 Academy Awards by winning all nine of its nominations—including Best Director—making Bertolucci the first and only Italian citizen to ever win that specific directing Oscar.

While researching his 1993 film Little Buddha, Bertolucci traveled extensively through Bhutan and Nepal, developing a deep, lifelong fascination with Tibetan Buddhism despite maintaining his staunch atheism.

During the May 1968 student riots in Paris, Bertolucci was present at the protests defending Henri Langlois's tenure at the Cinémathèque Française, an experience he explicitly recreated thirty-five years later in his 2003 film The Dreamers.
Despite his severe physical limitations, he directed his final film, the claustrophobic 2012 drama Me and You, entirely from his wheelchair after abandoning an initially planned 3D format.
The Cannes Film Festival inaugurated its Honorary Palme d'Or in 2011 by presenting the very first one to Bertolucci at the opening ceremony.

name: Bi Gan
name_meaning: Written as 毕赣, the surname Bi (毕) translates to 'completed' or 'finished', while Gan (赣) is the official character abbreviation for Jiangxi Province and the name of its principal river.
intro: Bi Gan is a visionary Chinese auteur known for his hypnotic, time-bending explorations of memory and regret. Rooted in his misty hometown of Kaili, his films blend raw realism with surreal, technically audacious long takes and his own original poetry.

facts.text: Raised in Kaili, Guizhou province, Bi grew up in an isolated, misty, subtropical mountainous region that would later serve as the inescapable, dreamlike setting for his major films.

While studying television directing at Shanxi Communication University, he watched Andrei Tarkovsky's 'Stalker' in a dingy internet cafe, initially finding it so boring he almost turned it off before realizing its poetic rhythm had fundamentally altered his perception of time.
He cast his real-life uncle, Chen Yongzhong—a former street tough who spent years in prison—as his frequent lead actor, utilizing his relative's world-weary aura to ground his surreal narratives.
He shot his debut feature, 'Kaili Blues', on a microscopic budget funded partly by his teacher, using a crew composed almost entirely of inexperienced college friends and local family members.

The famous 41-minute unbroken take in 'Kaili Blues' was filmed using a consumer-grade Panasonic Lumix GH4 camera mounted on a cheap stabilizer, physically passed between operators riding a motorcycle, boarding a boat, and running on foot.
Despite its extreme DIY origins, 'Kaili Blues' won Bi the Best Emerging Director award at the 2015 Locarno Film Festival, making him the youngest winner in the festival's history at age 26.
A published poet, Bi integrates his own original verses into his films, using them as voiceover devices to bridge the gap between his characters' waking lives and their subconscious dreams.

He insists on having his actors speak in the obscure Kaili dialect rather than standard Mandarin, a choice that roots the films in his childhood but requires subtitles even for native Chinese audiences.

For his sophomore film, 'Long Day's Journey Into Night', he orchestrated an astonishing 59-minute unbroken shot that required audiences to physically put on 3D glasses at the exact moment the protagonist enters a movie theater and falls asleep.

'Long Day's Journey Into Night' achieved a staggering $38 million opening day in China after marketers deceptively promoted it on the social media app Douyin (TikTok) as a romantic 'kiss at midnight' New Year's Eve date movie.
He frequently references the floating figures in Marc Chagall's paintings as the direct visual inspiration for the recurring, magical-realist motif of levitating characters in his films.

name: Billy Wilder
name_meaning: Born Samuel Wilder; 'Samuel' derives from the Hebrew שְׁמוּאֵל (Shmu'el), meaning 'God has heard', while the Germanic surname 'Wilder' denotes someone of an untamed nature. His mother nicknamed him 'Billie' (later Billy) due to her fascination with the American touring entertainer Buffalo Bill Cody.
intro: A razor-witted Austrian-Jewish refugee who escaped the Nazis to become Hollywood's most cynical storyteller, Billy Wilder weaponized his dark European sensibility to dismantle American taboos across film noir, screwball comedy, and searing social satire.

facts.text: Born Samuel Wilder in the Austro-Hungarian railway town of Sucha, he dropped out of the University of Vienna to become a journalist, famously securing a rare interview with Sigmund Freud who promptly kicked the young reporter out of his Berggasse 19 apartment.
To supplement his meager freelance writing income in 1920s Berlin, Wilder worked as a 'taxi dancer' at the Hotel Eden, where lonely older women paid him by the hour to dance the foxtrot and tango.

Fleeing Berlin for Paris immediately after Adolf Hitler's election in 1933, Wilder lived out of a cramped room at the Hotel Ansonia and co-directed his first film, the teen gang thriller *Mauvaise Graine*, shooting entirely on the streets because the crew could not afford studio space.

Arriving in Hollywood in 1934 with just eleven dollars and virtually no English vocabulary, he shared a squalid apartment with fellow refugee Peter Lorre and spent his days eating canned soup and listening to baseball broadcasts to learn American slang.

Wilder's mother Eugenia, his grandmother, and his stepfather were all murdered in the Holocaust, a tragedy he confirmed only after World War II when he returned to Germany as a U.S. Army colonel tasked with overseeing the denazification of the German entertainment industry.

His legendary twelve-year writing partnership with the patrician, Harvard-educated Republican Charles Brackett was famously volatile, with the two men screaming at each other daily and occasionally throwing telephone books across the room to settle plot disputes.

While co-writing the seminal film noir *Double Indemnity* in 1944, Wilder clashed bitterly with novelist Raymond Chandler, who was so offended by Wilder wearing a hat indoors and aggressively waving a riding crop that Chandler submitted a formal memo of complaint to Paramount executives.

For the iconic opening of *Sunset Boulevard*, Wilder originally filmed William Holden’s corpse chatting with other dead bodies in the Los Angeles County Morgue, but was forced to hastily reshoot the scene in a swimming pool after a preview audience in Evanston, Illinois, erupted into unintended laughter.

Wilder's acidic Hollywood critique *Sunset Boulevard* infuriated studio mogul Louis B. Mayer, who publicly screamed at Wilder after a screening, demanding he be 'tarred and feathered and run out of Hollywood' for biting the hand that fed him.

During the filming of *Sabrina*, star Humphrey Bogart despised Wilder and his co-star William Holden, derisively nicknaming the Jewish refugee director a 'Prussian Nazi' and pointedly inviting everyone except Wilder into his dressing room for evening drinks.

Wilder’s experience directing Marilyn Monroe in *Some Like It Hot* was so agonizing—requiring 47 takes for her to correctly deliver the three-word line 'It's me, Sugar'—that he was explicitly excluded from the cast's wrap party.

Despite his public exhaustion with Monroe's chronic lateness and pill addictions, Wilder fiercely defended her cinematic genius, noting that 'my Aunt Minnie would always be punctual and never hold up production, but who would pay to see my Aunt Minnie?'.
He amassed an extraordinary, multi-million-dollar private collection of modern art, purchasing early works by Pablo Picasso, Balthus, and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner with his Hollywood paychecks.

His longtime writing routine with I.A.L. Diamond involved Wilder pacing the office relentlessly for hours, wielding a swagger stick, while the quiet, methodical Diamond sat at a typewriter smoking cigarettes and acting as a filter for Wilder's rapid-fire ideas.

Fearing the impact of Wilder's bleak alcoholism drama *The Lost Weekend*, the American liquor industry allegedly offered Paramount Pictures $5 million to burn the film's negative, a proposition the studio rejected before the movie swept the Academy Awards.

In his later years, Wilder desperately wanted to direct an adaptation of Thomas Keneally's novel *Schindler's Ark* as a personal memorial to his family lost in the Holocaust, but Steven Spielberg had already secured the rights to direct *Schindler's List*.

Wilder was notoriously unsentimental about the mechanics of directing, openly admitting that he only stepped behind the camera to protect his own scripts from being ruined by other Hollywood filmmakers.

He discovered a young Audrey Hepburn for the lead in *Sabrina* and was so charmed by her that he altered the script daily to highlight her natural effervescence, cementing her transition from a European stage actress to a global fashion icon.

To achieve the perfect aesthetic of a desolate, frozen World War II prisoner-of-war camp for *Stalag 17*, Wilder forced his cast and crew to shoot on a miserably muddy, rain-soaked set in Calabasas, California.

He maintained a lifelong, brotherly friendship with actor William Holden, rescuing the actor's stalling career by casting him as the doomed gigolo Joe Gillis and later delivering the eulogy at Holden's funeral in 1981.

Disgusted by the self-indulgent camera tricks of the French New Wave, Wilder strictly adhered to a classical visual style, insisting that the audience should never consciously notice the camera moving.
Despite his reputation as a master of American vernacular, Wilder never lost his heavy Austro-Hungarian accent, often using his fractured pronunciation to disarm aggressive studio executives.

When he received the AFI Life Achievement Award in 1986, a visibly moved Wilder used his acceptance speech to thank the anonymous U.S. consul in Mexicali who had stamped his passport in 1934, legally allowing him to enter America to 'write some good ones'.

Wilder's ashes are interred at the Pierce Brothers Westwood Village Memorial Park in Los Angeles, resting beneath a tombstone that reads, 'I'm a writer but then nobody's perfect,' a direct homage to the famous final line of his comedy masterpiece *Some Like It Hot*.

name: Bong Joon Ho
name_meaning: Bong Joon-ho (봉준호 / 奉俊昊) translates roughly to 'a talented man who reveres the vast sky.' The surname Bong (奉) means 'to offer or revere,' Joon (俊) denotes 'talented or outstanding,' and Ho (昊) signifies 'the vast, summer sky.'
intro: A master of genre-blending social satire, Bong Joon Ho rose from South Korea's democratization movement to global cinematic dominance. Nicknamed 'Bong-tail' for his obsessive precision, he became the first Korean auteur to win the Palme d'Or and Best Picture.

facts.text: Bong's maternal grandfather, Park Tae-won, was a celebrated modernist novelist during the Japanese colonial era who defected to North Korea in 1950, making his legacy a strict taboo in South Korea for decades.

Raised in a highly intellectual household in Daegu, Bong grew up surrounded by vast collections of Western art books belonging to his father, Bong Sang-gyun, a prominent first-generation graphic designer.
While studying sociology at Yonsei University, he honed his visual storytelling by drawing a regular, politically charged comic strip for the campus newspaper, Yonsei Chunchu.

He met his wife, Jung Sun-young, in a university film club, and during his early struggling years as a filmmaker, she supported the household by working while he shot wedding videos to buy 16mm film stock.

He is universally known in the South Korean film industry by the nickname 'Bong-tail'—a portmanteau of his surname and the word 'detail'—due to his obsessive micromanagement of props and millimeter-precise framing.

When Bong was an assistant director on the 1997 film Motel Cactus, he had to reject a then-unknown Song Kang-ho but left such a polite, respectful voicemail that the actor promised to work with him in the future.

The inspiration for The Host struck Bong in high school when he looked out his apartment window and hallucinated a strange, Loch Ness-style creature dangling from one of the bridges spanning Seoul's Han River.

When notoriously heavy-handed executive Harvey Weinstein demanded he cut twenty minutes from Snowpiercer, Bong saved a crucial scene of a train guard gutting a fish by lying that the shot was a heartfelt tribute to his fisherman father.

Under the conservative administrations of Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, Bong was secretly placed on a government blacklist of over 9,000 artists deemed left-leaning or subversive, subjecting him to covert state surveillance.

At the 2020 Golden Globes, he famously chastised American cinematic insularity by declaring, 'Once you overcome the one-inch tall barrier of subtitles, you will be introduced to so many more amazing films.'

During the grueling, months-long Parasite awards campaign, he formed a viral, symbiotic partnership with his 25-year-old interpreter Sharon Choi, whom he publicly praised as a brilliant filmmaker in her own right.
He considers Alfred Hitchcock his supreme master, specifically studying the winding staircase sequences in Psycho and Vertigo to design the vertical architecture of class warfare in Parasite.
After sweeping the Oscars, Bong received a personal, handwritten letter from Martin Scorsese telling him to 'rest well, but don't rest for too long,' which Bong has since framed in his office.

name: Brad Bird
name_meaning: The name "Phillip" originates from the Greek Philippos (Φίλιππος), meaning "lover of horses." "Bradley" derives from the Old English words brad (broad) and leah (woodland clearing), while the surname "Bird" comes from the Old English bridd, historically used as an occupational name for a birdcatcher.
intro: A fiercely uncompromising visionary who bridged traditional Disney artistry and the Pixar CGI revolution, Brad Bird infuses his kinetic, deeply personal films with a recurring obsession: exceptional individuals rebelling against the suffocating constraints of enforced mediocrity.

facts.text: At age eleven, while on a family tour of the Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, Bird boldly broke away from the group to declare to legendary animators Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston that he would one day work for them.

Impressed by the Montana teenager's sheer audacity, Disney's notoriously prickly master animator Milt Kahl personally took Bird under his wing, mentoring him via harsh, exacting critiques mailed across the country.

Awarded a scholarship to the newly formed California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) by Disney, Bird shared a dorm room with future Pixar founder John Lasseter and attended classes alongside Tim Burton.

Despite achieving his childhood dream of working at Walt Disney Animation Studios in his twenties, Bird was unceremoniously fired by studio administrator Ed Hansen in 1981 for openly criticizing the company's safe, stagnant creative direction.
Following his dismissal from Disney, Bird briefly pivoted to live-action screenwriting, co-authoring the script for the 1987 Steven Spielberg-produced sci-fi film Batteries Not Included.

Bird played a crucial role in the early visual development of The Simpsons, directing the seminal 1990 episode "Krusty Gets Busted" and establishing the show's foundational cinematic language by treating the animated camera like a live-action lens.
In 1990, Bird also directed the music video for the hit rap single "Do the Bartman," bringing an unprecedented level of complex, MTV-style choreography to the animated cast of The Simpsons.

His first feature film, The Iron Giant, was born from profound personal tragedy: the tragic death of his older sister Susan, who was shot and killed by her estranged husband, prompting Bird to pitch the story with the central question, "What if a gun had a soul and didn't want to be a gun?"

The Iron Giant was produced at Warner Bros. Feature Animation during a period when the studio was actively shutting down its animation division, allowing Bird to work with unprecedented creative freedom because executives were largely ignoring his team.

When his former college roommate John Lasseter recruited him to Pixar to direct The Incredibles, Bird became the first outside director ever hired by the studio and the first to pitch a feature starring exclusively human characters.

Bird ended up voicing the iconic, eccentric costume designer Edna Mode in The Incredibles only after actress Lily Tomlin listened to his temporary scratch-track recording and bluntly told him she could not perform the role any better than he already had.

In 2005, Pixar executives asked Bird to urgently take over the troubled production of Ratatouille from original director Jan Pinkava, giving him only eighteen months to completely rewrite the script, redesign the characters, and finish the film.

He physically acts out the exact facial expressions and bodily movements he wants from his characters while directing, a highly theatrical habit he directly inherited from watching his mentor Milt Kahl at Disney.
Tom Cruise personally recruited Bird to make his live-action directorial debut with Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol after being mesmerized by the dynamic, kinetic camera work in The Incredibles.

Bird has frequently faced—and vehemently denied—accusations from film critics that his recurring cinematic themes of suppressed geniuses fighting against enforced mediocrity are secretly vehicles for Ayn Rand's Objectivist philosophy.

His 2015 live-action sci-fi film Tomorrowland was deeply inspired by his lifelong fascination with Walt Disney's original, mid-century utopian vision for the EPCOT center and the 1964 New York World's Fair.

He was formally offered the chance to direct Star Wars: Episode VII - The Force Awakens but turned down the highly coveted job to honor his prior commitment to finish Tomorrowland for George Clooney and Disney.

He routinely includes a hidden Easter egg of "A113"—the classroom number for graphic design students at CalArts—in his films, placing it on license plates, unlit train monitors, and even a protocol override code in Mission: Impossible.
He provided a vocal cameo in the 2015 blockbuster Jurassic World, serving as the cheerfully automated voice of the park's monorail announcer.

name: Brady Corbet
name_meaning: The surname Corbet is of Norman French origin, derived from 'corb' (meaning raven or crow), while the given name Brady stems from the Irish surname Mac Brádaigh, meaning 'descendant of Brádach' (translated as spirited, or broad-eyed).
intro: Brady Corbet transitioned from a disillusioned child actor into one of modern cinema’s most fiercely ambitious auteurs, utilizing his acting career as a European film school before directing uncompromising, celluloid-shot epics like Vox Lux and The Brutalist.

facts.text: Born in Scottsdale, Arizona, Corbet was raised by a single mother, Mary, and began his career as a child actor in television commercials at age seven before moving to Los Angeles to pursue film.
His first major cinematic role came at age fourteen in Catherine Hardwicke’s gritty teenage drama Thirteen (2003), playing the protagonist's brother, Mason.

A traumatic early brush with Hollywood blockbusters occurred when he starred as Alan Tracy in Jonathan Frakes's critical and commercial disaster Thunderbirds (2004), an experience that permanently soured the teenage actor on studio tentpoles.

Disillusioned with American commercial cinema, Corbet deliberately used his acting career as a de facto film school, actively seeking out roles with uncompromising European auteurs like Lars von Trier, Olivier Assayas, and Ruben Östlund to study their onset methods.

He made his directorial debut at age nineteen with the short film Protect You + Me (2008), which won an Honorable Mention at the Sundance Film Festival and signaled his formal pivot behind the camera.

Corbet met his long-term romantic and creative partner, Norwegian filmmaker Mona Fastvold, when he was cast in her directorial debut The Sleepwalker (2014); they have since co-written all three of his feature films.

Walker's thunderous, orchestral soundtrack for The Childhood of a Leader was one of the musician's final film scores, and Walker returned to score Corbet's sophomore feature Vox Lux (2018) shortly before his death in 2019.

Corbet's debut feature The Childhood of a Leader premiered at the 2015 Venice Film Festival, where the twenty-seven-year-old won both the Luigi De Laurentiis Award for a Debut Film and the Orizzonti Award for Best Director.

To capture the authentic feel of pop-star stadium performances in Vox Lux, Corbet enlisted Australian pop star Sia to write original, unreleased songs for Natalie Portman's character to perform on screen.

Driven by a monumental ambition rarely seen in modern independent cinema, Corbet chose to shoot The Brutalist on extremely rare VistaVision 35mm film stock, which was later blown up to 70mm for theatrical projection.
To stretch the film's modest budget, Corbet shot The Brutalist almost entirely in Hungary, constructing massive, brutalist architectural sets in local studios to double for post-war Pennsylvania.
The sprawling 215-minute runtime of The Brutalist includes a mandatory 15-minute intermission, a structural homage to the mid-century Hollywood epics of Corbet's cinematic heroes.
At the 2024 Venice Film Festival, the world premiere of The Brutalist was met with a rapturous 12-minute standing ovation, culminating in Corbet winning the Silver Lion for Best Director.

A lifelong cinephile, Corbet cites Robert Bresson, Carl Theodor Dreyer, and Stanley Kubrick as his primary cinematic deities, often structuring his own films with rigid, chapter-based architectural precision.

Corbet's three feature films form a thematic trilogy about the sociopolitical ruins of the 20th century forging monstrous megalomaniacs, spanning the aftermath of World War I in The Childhood of a Leader, post-9/11 pop culture in Vox Lux, and Holocaust survival in The Brutalist.

name: Brian De Palma
name_meaning: The name Brian is of Celtic origin, generally believed to mean 'high' or 'noble'. The Italian surname De Palma literally translates to 'of the palm tree', historically used to denote a pilgrim who had returned from the Holy Land carrying a palm frond.
intro: A master of cinematic suspense and visual flamboyance, Brian De Palma emerged from the New Hollywood movement to forge a controversial career defined by Hitchcockian voyeurism, split-screen virtuosity, and operatic violence.

facts.text: Raised in Philadelphia, a young De Palma frequently stood in the operating room watching his orthopedic surgeon father, Anthony De Palma, perform bloody amputations, an experience that inoculated the future director against the sight of extreme gore.

He enrolled at Columbia University to study physics, but after being mesmerized by campus screenings of Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo and Orson Welles’s Citizen Kane, he abandoned science to focus on the theater department.
In 1962, he became one of the very first male students to enroll at the historically women-only Sarah Lawrence College when he entered their newly established Master of Fine Arts program in theater.
While shooting his debut feature The Wedding Party in 1963, De Palma discovered an unknown, nineteen-year-old actor named Robert De Niro, accidentally crediting him as 'Robert Denero' due to a typo.

While directing the 1972 studio comedy Get to Know Your Rabbit, De Palma was so severely bullied by his cinematic idol, Orson Welles—who refused to memorize lines and demanded constant script changes—that the young director was briefly fired from his own film.
De Palma and his close friend George Lucas held joint casting sessions in 1975, with actors simultaneously auditioning for the high school roles in Carrie and the space-fantasy roles in Star Wars.

After attending a disastrous early screening of Star Wars without its special effects, an appalled De Palma ruthlessly mocked the confusing plot and personally helped Lucas rewrite the iconic opening text crawl to make the story comprehensible.

He coaxed legendary composer Bernard Herrmann out of retirement to score Sisters and Obsession, famously dealing with the irascible musician's tantrums, including Herrmann screaming at him for suggesting a track sounded like his old Hitchcock scores.
With his 1976 blockbuster Carrie, De Palma became the very first director to adapt a Stephen King novel for the screen, purchasing the rights when King was still a virtual unknown.
He married actress Nancy Allen in 1979 and made her his primary muse, casting her as a cynical prostitute in Dressed to Kill and a naive makeup artist in Blow Out before their divorce in 1983.

His thrillers Dressed to Kill and Body Double sparked furious protests from the feminist group Women Against Violence Against Women, who picketed theaters and accused De Palma of glorifying the sadistic murder of women.

While directing Scarface, De Palma repeatedly clashed with the film's screenwriter, Oliver Stone, eventually banning Stone from the set because the writer kept giving unsolicited acting notes to Al Pacino.

Desperate for a commercial hit after the financial failure of Blow Out, De Palma agreed to direct the music video for Bruce Springsteen’s 'Dancing in the Dark,' famously casting a young Courteney Cox as the fan pulled onto the stage.

When Paramount refused to fund an expensive train-yard shootout for The Untouchables, De Palma improvised the sequence on a staircase at Chicago's Union Station, borrowing the bouncing baby carriage motif from Sergei Eisenstein’s Battleship Potemkin.
In 1991, he married powerful Hollywood producer Gale Anne Hurd—who had recently divorced James Cameron—and she produced his psychological thriller Raising Cain before they too divorced.

Tom Cruise personally recruited De Palma to direct the first Mission: Impossible film in 1996, but De Palma adamantly refused to return for the sequel, telling Cruise that directing one blockbuster in a franchise was more than enough.

The iconic, tension-filled scene in Mission: Impossible where Tom Cruise dangles from a wire in a silent CIA vault was entirely De Palma's invention, designed specifically to create a suspense sequence devoid of dialogue or gunfire.
His entire career, complete with brutal honesty about his flops and feuds, was chronicled in the acclaimed 2015 documentary De Palma, directed by his ardent admirers Noah Baumbach and Jake Paltrow.

For the opening of the 1998 thriller Snake Eyes, De Palma orchestrated a massively complex, 12-minute continuous tracking shot following Nicolas Cage through an Atlantic City boxing arena, though he secretly stitched multiple takes together using digital effects.

He originally hired Bob Hoskins to play Al Capone in The Untouchables because Robert De Niro was wavering, and when De Niro finally accepted the role, De Palma sent a grateful Hoskins a $200,000 'pay or play' check just for stepping aside.

His 1974 rock opera Phantom of the Paradise was a colossal box office bomb in the United States but inexplicably became a massive cultural phenomenon in Winnipeg, Manitoba, where it played continuously in theaters for months.

He spent twenty years trying to adapt Daniel Lang's New Yorker article about a Vietnam War atrocity into the 1989 film Casualties of War, only to watch stars Michael J. Fox and Sean Penn genuinely despise each other on set.

The disastrous production of his 1990 adaptation of Tom Wolfe's The Bonfire of the Vanities was so chaotic it spawned Julie Salamon's bestselling behind-the-scenes book The Devil's Candy, which remains one of the most revealing accounts of a Hollywood flop ever written.

name: Carl Theodor Dreyer
name_meaning: The name Carl derives from the Germanic word 'karlaz' meaning 'free man,' while Theodor comes from the Greek 'Theodōros,' meaning 'gift of God.' The surname Dreyer is an occupational name of Middle Low German origin, referring to a woodturner.
intro: A towering figure of early cinema, Carl Theodor Dreyer channeled his traumatic, loveless childhood into austere, spiritually agonizing masterpieces. Renowned for his tyrannical perfectionism, he spent decades relentlessly pursuing an unrealized film about Jesus Christ before dying unexpectedly.

facts.text: Dreyer was born out of wedlock in Copenhagen to a married Danish estate manager, Jens Christian Torp, and his Swedish housekeeper, Josephine Bernhardine Nilsson, who gave him up for adoption to hide the affair.

He was adopted by a strictly Lutheran typographer, Carl Theodor Dreyer Sr., and his wife Inger Marie, who emotionally abused the boy by constantly reminding him that he should be grateful for his food given his illegitimate origins.

Before entering cinema, he worked as an aggressive young journalist under the pen name 'Tommen' for the newspaper Ekstra Bladet, specializing in exposing municipal scandals and writing aviation reports.

He financed his eerie 1932 early sound film Vampyr entirely through the patronage of a wealthy young Dutch aristocrat, Nicolas de Gunzburg, in exchange for casting the inexperienced baron in the lead role under the pseudonym 'Julian West.'
In 1949, Dreyer signed a contract with an American producer to make a film about the life of Jesus Christ, sparking a manic, two-decade obsession that would consume the rest of his life and career.
To ensure absolute historical and linguistic accuracy for his unrealized Jesus film, Dreyer taught himself to read Hebrew and made multiple extensive research trips to Israel.

Because of his uncompromising nature and the massive gaps between his directing projects, Dreyer supported his family for the last sixteen years of his life by working as the manager of the Dagmar Teatret, a prominent cinema in Copenhagen.

Shortly after premiering Day of Wrath during the Nazi occupation of Denmark, Dreyer sold the film rights to a Swedish distributor and used the pretext of a business trip to flee across the Øresund to neutral Sweden, where he stayed until the end of World War II.
While in Swedish exile, he directed Two People (1945), a film he immediately disowned because the Svensk Filmindustri studio forced him to cast an actor he considered completely wrong for the part.

The premiere of his final film, Gertrud (1964), at the Paris Opera was a notorious disaster, with half the audience walking out in protest of its glacial pacing and the remaining viewers violently booing at the end.

After nineteen years of relentless effort, Dreyer finally secured the $3 million budget required to shoot his Jesus film from Italian state television in early 1968, but he died of pneumonia just weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

name: Celine Sciamma
name_meaning: "Céline" derives from the Latin "Caelina," meaning "heavenly" or "of the sky." "Sciamma" is an Italian Jewish surname of Levantine and Sephardic origin, likely derived from the Arabic "shamma" (fragrance) or the Hebrew "shamash" (a synagogue servant or candle-maker).
intro: Céline Sciamma is a pioneering French filmmaker who has redefined the cinematic "female gaze." Emerging from the Parisian suburbs, she crafts meticulously observed, fiercely intimate portraits of girlhood, queer desire, and women's hidden inner lives.

facts.text: Before pursuing filmmaking, she harboured dreams of becoming a literary critic and earned a master's degree in French literature from Paris Nanterre University.
She originally attended the prestigious La Fémis film school solely to study screenwriting, having absolutely no ambition to become a director until her graduation year.

Sciamma relies almost exclusively on the electronic musician Jean-Baptiste de Laubier, known professionally as Para One, whom she met at La Fémis and who has composed the pulsating, anachronistic scores for nearly all her films.

She wrote the screenplay for her gender-bending sophomore feature *Tomboy* in a frenetic three-week sprint, rushing the production into a 20-day shoot to capture the fleeting summer weather and the exact physical awkwardness of her child actors.

Sciamma is a leading architect of the modern cinematic "female gaze," actively removing the male perspective from her sets; her period masterpiece *Portrait of a Lady on Fire* features virtually no men on screen after the opening minutes.

Despite writing *Portrait of a Lady on Fire* specifically for Adèle Haenel, the couple amicably ended their romantic relationship before filming began, turning the production into a profound, collaborative processing of their own real-life breakup.

A prominent activist for gender equality in the French film industry, Sciamma co-founded the Collectif 50/50, which successfully pressured the Cannes Film Festival to sign a pledge for gender parity in its executive ranks.

At the 45th César Awards in 2020, Sciamma made international headlines when she and Haenel staged a dramatic walkout from the Salle Pleyel to protest Roman Polanski winning Best Director, with Haenel shouting "Shame!" as they exited.

Beyond her own directorial projects, she is a highly sought-after script doctor and co-writer, earning an Academy Award nomination for adapting the stop-motion animated film *My Life as a Zucchini* for director Claude Barras.
She also co-wrote the screenplay for Jacques Audiard's black-and-white millennial drama *Paris, 13th District*, adapting the graphic novels of American cartoonist Adrian Tomine.

Early in her career, she helped develop and co-write the first drafts of the acclaimed supernatural television series *The Returned* (Les Revenants) before leaving the project to focus on directing *Tomboy*.

She frequently casts non-professional actors scouted from the streets or shopping malls of Paris, a technique she used extensively to find the vibrant teenage ensemble, including star Karidja Touré, for *Girlhood*.

During the casting of *Petite Maman*, she miraculously found real-life twin sisters Joséphine and Gabrielle Sanz to play the mother and daughter, leaning into their natural biological bond to anchor the film's magical-realist premise.
She considers David Lynch's *Mulholland Drive* her ultimate cinematic touchstone, often revisiting its surreal, dreamlike exploration of female identity before starting a new project.

name: Chad Stahelski
name_meaning: The English given name Chad is derived from the Old English 'Ceadda', which traces back to the Welsh root 'cad', meaning 'battle' or 'warrior'. His surname, Stahelski, is of Polish origin and derives from the word 'stal', meaning 'steel', historically denoting an ancestor who was a steelworker or a person of unyielding character.
intro: Chad Stahelski transitioned from an elite shootfighter and Keanu Reeves's stunt double to a visionary director who revolutionized Hollywood action. By blending Hong Kong choreography with classical mythology, he redefined the modern blockbuster through the John Wick franchise.

facts.text: Stahelski began his martial arts journey at age ten after watching Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon, eventually training extensively at the Inosanto Academy under Dan Inosanto, Lee's legendary protégé.
Stahelski’s breakthrough in Hollywood came under tragic circumstances when he was hired as the stunt double for Brandon Lee on Alex Proyas's gothic thriller The Crow in 1993.
Following Brandon Lee’s fatal on-set shooting, Stahelski stepped in as Lee’s stand-in to complete the film, with special effects artists mapping Lee's face onto Stahelski's body for the final scenes.

He auditioned for The Matrix in 1997 by enduring a grueling hour-and-a-half physical test overseen by Hong Kong choreography legend Yuen Woo-ping, which included non-stop kicks, flips, and exhaustive wire-work drills.

Stahelski won the role of Keanu Reeves's stunt double for The Matrix partly because his physical proportions perfectly matched the actor, sparking a decades-long creative partnership and close personal friendship.

In 1997, Stahelski and fellow stuntman David Leitch co-founded 87Eleven Action Design, transforming a sprawling Inglewood warehouse into an elite 'action dojo' where A-list actors undergo months of relentless martial arts conditioning.

He served as the martial arts stunt coordinator for The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, directly choreographing the iconic, rain-soaked 'Burly Brawl' between Neo and dozens of Agent Smiths.

Stahelski's transition to directing was initiated by Keanu Reeves, who sent him Derek Kolstad's script for a film then titled Scorn, asking if 87Eleven could handle the action design, to which Stahelski replied by pitching himself as the director.

Because of strict Directors Guild of America rules regarding co-directing credits, Stahelski received sole directorial credit on the original John Wick (2014), while his collaborator David Leitch was credited only as a producer.

He heavily incorporates his love for classical dance and musical theater into his action choreography, frequently citing Bob Fosse and Gene Kelly as primary influences for how he frames full-body movement and rhythm.

Stahelski insists on shooting action in wide angles with long, unbroken takes—a deliberate rejection of the 'shaky-cam' and rapid-cut style popularized by the Bourne franchise, drawing instead from Hong Kong cinema and Buster Keaton.
He was previously married to fellow elite stunt performer Heidi Moneymaker, who is best known as the longtime stunt double for Scarlett Johansson's Black Widow in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

As a lifelong fan of anime and manga, Stahelski has actively developed live-action adaptations of properties like Ghost of Tsushima and frequently cites Shinichirō Watanabe's Cowboy Bebop as a stylistic touchstone.
Stahelski is deeply obsessed with Greek mythology and Arthurian legends, intentionally structuring the John Wick sequels around classical motifs of the Underworld, high tables, and inescapable fate.

He actively pushes to elevate the recognition of stunt performers in Hollywood, publicly campaigning for the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to introduce an Oscar category specifically for stunt coordination.

Stahelski occasionally returns to his roots to direct second-unit action sequences for other filmmakers even after becoming a successful main-unit director, notably contributing to blockbuster productions like The Hunger Games: Catching Fire and Captain America: Civil War.
He is a self-professed fanatic of Russell Mulcahy's 1986 fantasy film Highlander, utilizing his industry clout to secure the directorial rights for a reboot starring Henry Cavill.

To achieve the neon-drenched aesthetic of the John Wick franchise, Stahelski works closely with cinematographer Dan Laustsen, utilizing extreme color palettes inspired by Italian Giallo films and the works of Dario Argento.

name: Chris Columbus
name_meaning: The name 'Christopher' is derived from the Greek 'Christophoros' (Χριστόφορος), meaning 'Christ-bearer.' His surname 'Columbus' is an Anglicized form of the Latin 'columba,' meaning 'dove.'
intro: A master of the modern family blockbuster, Chris Columbus channeled his working-class Ohio roots and childhood anxieties into generation-defining hits. As a writer, director, and producer, he shaped the cinematic landscapes of Gremlins, Home Alone, and Harry Potter.

facts.text: Born in Spangler, Pennsylvania, Columbus was raised in Champion, Ohio, by a factory-worker mother and a father who labored in an aluminum plant and a coal mine.

While studying at NYU alongside classmate Charlie Kaufman, Columbus lived in a squalid, roach-and-rodent-infested Manhattan loft, an experience of hearing creatures scurrying in the dark that directly inspired his screenplay for Gremlins.

His original spec script for Gremlins was a dark, R-rated horror film in which the monsters decapitate the mother and eat the family dog, but Steven Spielberg purchased the script and convinced Columbus to soften the tone for a wider audience.
Spielberg's mentorship proved highly lucrative for the young writer, leading Columbus to pen both The Goonies and Young Sherlock Holmes for Amblin Entertainment.
He channeled his experiences as an outcast teenager in a bleak Ohio steel town into his first produced screenplay, the 1984 James Foley drama Reckless.

Columbus was originally hired to direct National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation but quit the project after two disastrous meetings with star Chevy Chase, who treated the young director with extreme condescension.
Although he cast Macaulay Culkin in Home Alone based on the boy's performance in Hughes's Uncle Buck, Columbus still auditioned hundreds of other children just to ensure he wasn't making a mistake.

On the set of Mrs. Doubtfire, Columbus used up to three cameras simultaneously to capture Robin Williams's rapid-fire improvisations, knowing the actor would rarely perform a comedic take the same way twice.
He and Williams formed such a close bond that they spent years developing a Mrs. Doubtfire sequel, a project Columbus permanently canceled following Williams's tragic death in 2014.

Columbus was so physically and emotionally exhausted by the back-to-back, 320-day shoots of the first two Harry Potter films that he stepped down from directing Prisoner of Azkaban to save his marriage and spend time with his children.
He has a long-standing tradition of casting his own children in cameo roles, most notably having his daughter Eleanor play Hufflepuff student Susan Bones in the first two Harry Potter films.

He directed the 2005 film adaptation of the Broadway musical Rent because he had been deeply moved by the stage production, having personally lived in the same gritty, impoverished 1980s New York neighborhoods depicted in Jonathan Larson's story.

In a stark departure from his family-friendly blockbuster image, Columbus co-founded Maiden Voyage Pictures with his daughter Eleanor, a production company that championed bleak, auteur-driven horror films like Robert Eggers's The Witch and The Lighthouse.
A lifelong Marvel fan who collected comics as a child, Columbus was heavily courted to direct the 2002 blockbuster Spider-Man before the studio ultimately hired Sam Raimi.

He was highly critical of the 2021 Disney+ reboot Home Sweet Home Alone, publicly stating that remaking a classic is a 'waste of time' and that the original's lightning-in-a-bottle magic could never be replicated.

name: Christian Petzold
name_meaning: "Christian" derives from the Latin "Christianus," meaning a follower of Christ. "Petzold" is a German surname originating as a diminutive of "Peter," which traces back to the Greek "petros," meaning rock or stone.
intro: A leading figure of the Berlin School, Christian Petzold creates haunting, meticulously framed cinema about ghosts, historical trauma, and transient identities. Deeply influenced by his parents' East German exile, he masterfully transposes classic genre tropes into fractured modern German landscapes.

facts.text: Born in the West German town of Hilden in 1960 to parents who had recently fled the German Democratic Republic, Petzold spent his childhood summers visiting relatives back in the East, instilling a lifelong fascination with borders and phantom identities.

During his mandatory civilian service as a conscientious objector, he ran a YMCA cinema club where he obsessively screened double bills of American genre films and European art-house classics, sparking his cinephilia.
Before turning to filmmaking, he moved to West Berlin in 1981 to study German literature and theater at the Free University, immersing himself in Marxist theory and structuralist thinkers.

While studying at the German Film and Television Academy Berlin (DFFB), he met the experimental documentary filmmaker Harun Farocki, who evolved from his strict professor into his closest friend and co-writer for the next two decades.

Alongside his DFFB classmates Thomas Arslan and Angela Schanelec, Petzold became a founding pillar of the "Berlin School" (Berliner Schule), a cinematic movement characterized by rigorous, unvarnished observations of post-reunification Germany, though he personally despised the label.

He has collaborated with cinematographer Hans Fromm on nearly every single one of his films since his 1995 graduation feature "Pilotinnen," developing a signature visual style of static, meticulously framed, and brightly lit shots.

Petzold found his ultimate cinematic muse in actress Nina Hoss, collaborating with her on six films—including "Yella," "Jerichow," and "Phoenix"—often casting her as a traumatized, enigmatic woman navigating a fractured Germany.

His 2008 film "Jerichow" is a direct, uncredited transposition of James M. Cain's hardboiled American crime novel "The Postman Always Rings Twice," relocated to the desolate, post-industrial landscape of northeastern Germany.

He won the Silver Bear for Best Director at the 2012 Berlin International Film Festival for "Barbara," a tense thriller about a banished East German doctor that finally brought his work to widespread international prominence.

For his acclaimed 2014 post-WWII drama "Phoenix," Petzold drew heavy inspiration from Hubert Monteilhet’s novel "Return from the Ashes," creating a haunting allegory for Germany's psychological refusal to look at its own Holocaust survivors.

The sudden death of his mentor and co-writer Harun Farocki in 2014 left Petzold creatively paralyzed, forcing him to abandon their final planned collaboration and fundamentally rethink his approach to filmmaking.

To break his creative block, he adapted Anna Seghers' 1944 novel "Transit," making the radical, disorienting choice to film a World War II refugee story in the modern-day streets of Marseille without altering the period dialogue.

Following the end of his collaborative era with Nina Hoss, Petzold discovered a new muse in Paula Beer during the casting of "Transit," initiating a second major phase of his career built entirely around her performances.

Seeking a new structural framework after Farocki's death, Petzold embarked on a trilogy inspired by the classical elements and German romantic myths, beginning with the element of water in his 2020 modern fairytale "Undine."

In March 2020, Petzold contracted a severe early case of COVID-19 while in Paris, and his subsequent fever dreams of being trapped in a burning forest directly inspired the screenplay for his fire-element film, "Afire."

An obsessive collector of vinyl records, he famously structured the emotional climax of "Afire" around the melancholic Austrian pop song "in my mind" by Wallners, playing it live on set to dictate the actors' physical rhythm.

Critics often group his early 2000s films "The State I Am In," "Ghosts," and "Yella" into a "Gespenster-Trilogie" (Ghost Trilogy), reflecting his obsession with characters who wander through modern capitalist Germany as if they are already dead.

Unlike many contemporary art-house auteurs, Petzold has never shied away from television, frequently directing episodes for the long-running German police procedural "Polizeiruf 110" to keep his directing muscles sharp between feature films.

He is a massive fan of American cinema and frequently borrows elements from Alfred Hitchcock, most notably in "Phoenix," which functions as a profound inversion of the psychological obsession depicted in "Vertigo."

name: Christopher Nolan
name_meaning: Christopher derives from the Greek 'Christophoros' (Χριστόφορος), meaning 'Christ-bearer'. Nolan comes from the Irish surname 'Ó Nualláin', meaning 'descendant of Nuallán', a diminutive of 'nuall' which translates to 'noble, famous, or loud shout'.
intro: A champion of celluloid and practical effects, Christopher Nolan redefined the modern blockbuster by marrying cerebral, non-linear storytelling with massive studio budgets. His uncompromising vision has yielded some of the 21st century's most acclaimed and commercially successful cinematic spectacles.

facts.text: He began making films at age seven using his father's Super 8 camera and a cast of Star Wars action figures to shoot a stop-motion homage titled Space Wars.

Treating filmmaking as a formal profession, Nolan wears a tailored suit, waistcoat, and heavy overcoat on set every single day, a habit born from his time wearing uniforms at the Haileybury boarding school.

Rather than using CGI for the massive dust bowl farm in Interstellar (2014), Nolan planted 500 acres of real corn outside Calgary, Canada, and after filming wrapped, he harvested and sold the crop for a profit.

For the airport heist sequence in Tenet (2020), Nolan purchased a decommissioned Boeing 747 airplane and physically crashed it into a hangar in Victorville, California, calculating that the real stunt was cheaper than building miniatures or using digital effects.

Though Cillian Murphy failed his screen test for the role of Bruce Wayne in Batman Begins (2005), Nolan was so mesmerized by the actor's striking blue eyes inside the Batsuit that he immediately cast him as the villainous Scarecrow instead.

After a two-decade partnership with Warner Bros., Nolan publicly severed ties with the studio in 2020, furiously calling their new HBO Max platform 'the worst streaming service' after they announced day-and-date digital releases for their entire 2021 theatrical slate.

He enforces a strict 'no Ugg boots' policy for crew members on his sets, demanding professional footwear, and strongly discourages the presence of chairs around the video monitors to keep everyone physically engaged.
His legendary collaboration with composer Hans Zimmer temporarily ended when Zimmer chose to score Denis Villeneuve's Dune (2021) instead of Nolan's Tenet, prompting Nolan to hire Ludwig Göransson.

For the Trinity Test sequence in Oppenheimer, Nolan refused to use CGI for the atomic explosion, instead working with visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson to create a massive practical blast in the New Mexico desert using a mixture of magnesium, aluminum powder, and gasoline.

name: Claire Denis
name_meaning: The name Claire is of French origin, derived from the Latin 'clarus,' meaning 'clear,' 'bright,' or 'famous.' The surname Denis is the French form of the Latin 'Dionysius,' tracing back to the Greek god of wine and revelry, Dionysos.
intro: Claire Denis is a pioneering French auteur celebrated for her tactile, elliptical cinema that explores colonialism, marginalization, and the physical body. Raised in colonial Africa, she translates the friction of geographic and emotional displacement into profoundly sensory cinematic experiences.

facts.text: Raised across French colonial Africa—including Senegal, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, and Djibouti—Denis moved every two years as her father was a French civil servant stationed in the shrinking empire.

Despite his role in the colonial administration, her father was a staunch anti-colonialist who gave Denis a copy of Frantz Fanon’s radical text 'The Wretched of the Earth' when she was just 14 years old.

She initially studied economics in Paris, but her husband encouraged her to abandon the subject and apply to the prestigious film school IDHEC, where she was accepted and began her formal cinematic education.

Before directing her own work, she spent years as an assistant director for prominent filmmakers, forming a particularly deep bond with Wim Wenders while working on 'Paris, Texas' and 'Wings of Desire'.

She worked as an assistant director on Jim Jarmusch’s 'Down by Law', and Jarmusch later returned the favor by appearing in a cameo in her 1989 documentary about a Cameroonian music group, 'Man No Run'.

She initially wanted her directorial debut to be an adaptation of Doris Lessing's Rhodesian novel 'The Grass Is Singing', but when she couldn't secure the rights, she drew on her own childhood memories to write 'Chocolat'.
At IDHEC, she met cinematographer Agnès Godard, sparking a legendary collaboration that has spanned decades and defined the highly tactile, skin-focused visual style of her films.

Her masterpiece 'Beau Travail' was loosely adapted from Herman Melville’s 'Billy Budd', but Denis transposed the maritime tragedy to the French Foreign Legion in Djibouti, drawing on memories of the soldiers she watched as a child.

Her 2001 film 'Trouble Every Day', starring Vincent Gallo as an American afflicted by a cannibalistic sexual virus, caused mass walkouts and fainting at the Cannes Film Festival due to its extreme gore.

She collaborated directly with the prominent French philosopher Jean-Luc Nancy to make 'L'Intrus' (2004), a fragmented, dreamlike film inspired by his autobiographical essay about receiving a heart transplant.
She maintains a tight-knit "family" of recurring actors, most notably Alex Descas and Isaach de Bankolé, whom she casts repeatedly to explore the nuances of the Black diaspora in France.
Though strictly a director, she has made rare acting cameos for her friends, such as playing a frustrated mother in Tonie Marshall’s 1996 comedy 'Enfants de salaud'.

After decades of avoiding each other in the French film industry due to mutual intimidation, she finally teamed up with Juliette Binoche for 'Let the Sunshine In' (2017), a comedy loosely based on Roland Barthes' 'A Lover's Discourse'.

'35 Shots of Rum' was conceived as a direct homage to Yasujirō Ozu’s 'Late Spring', relocating the story of a widowed father and his devoted daughter to a community of train conductors in the Parisian suburbs.

Despite being a giant of French cinema for over 30 years, she did not win a major prize at the Cannes Film Festival until 2022, when she shared the Grand Prix for her Nicaragua-set thriller 'Stars at Noon'.
She co-writes almost all of her films with Jean-Pol Fargeau, often retreating to the French countryside where they cook together and talk for days before writing a single word.

name: Clint Eastwood
name_meaning: The given name Clinton derives from Old English, meaning a 'settlement on the hill' or 'cliff town' (from *klint* and *tūn*). The surname Eastwood is an Old English topographic name given to a person who lived near the eastern wood (*ēast* + *wudu*).
intro: An iconic actor who redefined the American antihero, Clint Eastwood evolved into an Oscar-winning director renowned for his ruthlessly efficient, unvarnished filmmaking. His career spans seven decades, marked by fierce independence, jazz composition, and a legendary 'one-take' style.

facts.text: Born during the Great Depression at Saint Francis Memorial Hospital in San Francisco, he weighed a massive eleven pounds and six ounces, prompting the maternity ward nurses to nickname him "Samson."

While serving as a swimming instructor at Fort Ord during the Korean War, he survived the crash of a Douglas AD bomber into the freezing Pacific Ocean by swimming two miles through kelp beds to the shore at Point Reyes.

Before finding acting success, he worked a string of grueling manual jobs across the Pacific Northwest, including baling hay, logging in Springfield, Oregon, and tending blast furnaces for Bethlehem Steel.
Universal Pictures dropped him from his first acting contract in 1955, allegedly because studio executives felt his Adam's apple protruded too much and he delivered his lines far too slowly.
Director Sergio Leone only cast him as the iconic "Man with No Name" in A Fistful of Dollars after established stars Richard Harrison, James Coburn, and Charles Bronson all rejected the $15,000 role.

Because he developed a deep hatred for loud noises startling the horses on Western sets, he famously never yells "Action!" or "Cut!" as a director, preferring to murmur a gentle "Go ahead" and "That's enough."

Known in Hollywood as a ruthlessly efficient director who routinely finishes shoots under budget, he rarely films more than one or two takes per setup, a strict rebellion against the agonizing perfectionism of directors like Sergio Leone.

After he controversially fired director Philip Kaufman from the set of The Outlaw Josey Wales and took over the film himself, the Directors Guild of America instituted the "Eastwood Rule," which permanently bans an actor or producer from firing a director to assume their duties.

Frustrated by local zoning laws that prevented him from building an office building, he ran for Mayor of Carmel-by-the-Sea, California, in 1986, winning by a landslide and successfully overturning the town's famously absurd ban on selling ice cream cones.

In his sixties, he was contacted by a woman named Laurie Murray, who had been given up for adoption by a woman Eastwood had a brief affair with in Seattle in 1953; he embraced her, and she subsequently became a regular presence at his family gatherings and film premieres.

Deeply traumatized by the sudden death of his father from a heart attack at age sixty-four, he adopted an intensely strict regimen of daily exercise, Transcendental Meditation, and a heavily plant-based diet that he has maintained since the 1970s.

His bitter fourteen-year relationship with actress Sondra Locke ended in a spectacular palimony lawsuit where he notoriously changed the locks on their Bel-Air home, packed her belongings into boxes, and eventually settled by securing her a bogus directing contract at Warner Bros. that yielded zero films.

A lifelong jazz aficionado who originally wanted to be a musician and idolized Charlie Parker, he composed the piano-driven orchestral scores for several of his own major films, including Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, and Changeling.

Following Sean Connery's departure from the franchise, producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman offered Eastwood the role of James Bond, but he firmly declined, insisting the British spy should only be played by an Englishman.

He purchased the script for Unforgiven from writer David Webb Peoples in the early 1980s but deliberately shelved the project for a full decade until he felt his face had aged enough to believably portray the weary, washed-up gunslinger William Munny.

At the 2012 Republican National Convention in Tampa, he delivered a widely mocked, heavily improvised speech where he spent twelve minutes arguing with an empty chair representing President Barack Obama.

At the age of eighty-three, he saved the life of tournament director Steve John at the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am by noticing the man choking on a piece of cheese and successfully performing the Heimlich maneuver.
He made his directorial debut with the 1971 psychological thriller Play Misty for Me, shooting the entire film in his beloved town of Carmel and completing it four days ahead of schedule.

name: Damien Chazelle
name_meaning: The name Damien is derived from the Greek name Damianos (Δαμιανός), stemming from the verb 'damao' (δαμάω) meaning 'to tame' or 'to subdue'. The surname Chazelle is a French topographic name derived from the Late Latin 'casella', a diminutive of 'casa', meaning a small house or hut.
intro: Damien Chazelle is an Oscar-winning American film director and screenwriter whose rhythm-driven, kinetically charged films frequently explore the brutal, obsessive sacrifices required to achieve artistic greatness, particularly within the worlds of jazz and classical Hollywood.
