His student documentary 'Hated: GG Allin and the Murder Junkies' (1993), about the notoriously self-destructive punk performer GG Allin, became one of NYU's highest-grossing student films and helped launch his career.
GG Allin died of a heroin overdose in 1993 just as Phillips was finishing the film, an ending the documentary captures around the singer's chaotic final concert.

His next documentary, 'Frat House' (1998), co-directed with Andrew Gurland, won the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival but was shelved by HBO amid disputes over how its hazing scenes were staged.
He made his narrative feature debut with 'Road Trip' (2000), produced by 'Animal House' veteran Ivan Reitman's company.
'The Hangover' (2009) was made on a modest budget yet grossed over $467 million worldwide, becoming one of the highest-grossing R-rated comedies ever at the time.
He shot much of 'The Hangover' in real Las Vegas locations including Caesars Palace, whose owners initially balked at the script's debauchery.
He cast then-unknown Zach Galifianakis as Alan after seeing his idiosyncratic stand-up comedy, a choice the studio resisted.
He publicly declared he was 'done with comedy' around 2019, telling interviewers that 'woke culture' had made it hard to be funny, a remark that drew significant backlash.
He pitched 'Joker' to Warner Bros. as a gritty character study modeled on 1970s films, explicitly citing Martin Scorsese's 'Taxi Driver' and 'The King of Comedy' as touchstones.
Martin Scorsese was attached as a producer on 'Joker' early in development before stepping away, though his influence remained central to the film's aesthetic.
'Joker' (2019) became the first R-rated film to gross over $1 billion at the global box office.
'Joker' premiered at the 76th Venice International Film Festival in 2019 and won the Golden Lion, the festival's top prize.
He earned Academy Award nominations for Best Director and, with Scott Silver, Best Adapted Screenplay for 'Joker,' which won two Oscars including Best Actor for Joaquin Phoenix.
He co-wrote 'Borat' (2006) and received an Oscar nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay, though he had departed the project's direction before filming.
He fell out with Sacha Baron Cohen during early work on 'Borat,' reportedly clashing over the dangerous, improvised guerrilla style of shooting.
Lady Gaga starred as Harley Quinn in his sequel 'Joker: Folie à Deux' (2024), which reimagined the franchise partly as a jukebox musical.
'Joker: Folie à Deux' was a notorious commercial and critical disappointment, recouping only a fraction of its predecessor's reception despite a reported budget exceeding $190 million.
He directed the action film 'War Dogs' (2016), based on a true Rolling Stone story about young Miami arms dealers played by Jonah Hill and Miles Teller.
His pivot from raunchy comedies to a prestige supervillain drama is one of the more startling reinventions in contemporary Hollywood, taking him from 'Road Trip' to a Golden Lion in two decades.

name: Tsai Ming-liang
name_meaning: 蔡明亮: the surname 蔡 (Cài) is an ancient Chinese clan name originally referring to the state of Cai in the Zhou dynasty; the given name 明亮 (Míngliàng) literally means 'bright' or 'luminous,' combining 明 (bright/clear) and 亮 (light/shining).
intro: Malaysian-born Taiwanese auteur of the 'slow cinema' movement, celebrated for near-wordless films of urban loneliness, leaking water and his muse Lee Kang-sheng; a Golden Lion winner who later turned to museums and walking.

facts.text: He was born in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak on the island of Borneo, in what is now Malaysia, to Chinese immigrant parents who ran a noodle stall.
As a young child he was largely raised by his maternal grandparents, who were obsessive cinema-goers and took him to watch as many as several films a day in Kuching's old movie houses.

This childhood immersion in the dark of cheap Kuching cinemas — often watching Hong Kong and Mandarin melodramas with his grandfather — became the wellspring of his lifelong nostalgia for the dying ritual of moviegoing.
He left Borneo at age twenty in 1977 to study at the Chinese Culture University (文化大學) in Taipei, enrolling in its Department of Drama and Cinema.
Before he ever directed for cinema he worked extensively in Taiwanese television, writing and directing TV dramas and stage plays through the 1980s.
His entire career pivoted on a chance encounter in 1991, when he spotted a teenager named Lee Kang-sheng (李康生) loitering in a Taipei video-game arcade and cast him on the spot.
Lee Kang-sheng has appeared in essentially every one of his feature films, becoming one of cinema's most enduring director-actor collaborations, spanning more than three decades.
His debut feature 'Rebels of the Neon God' (1992) grew directly out of that arcade discovery and the world of disaffected Taipei youth.
His 1994 film 'Vive L'Amour' won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, sharing the honour with Milcho Manchevski's 'Before the Rain.'
Lee Kang-sheng's real-life chronic neck pain inspired the entire film 'The River' (1997), in which his character suffers a mysterious, agonizing neck affliction.
Water — leaking ceilings, floods, rain, dripping pipes, tears — is the obsessive recurring motif across his filmography, a visual signature of bodies and apartments in slow disintegration.

His 'The Hole' (1998) was commissioned for a French television series marking the approach of the millennium, and he punctuated its bleak setting with surreal musical numbers using songs of Grace Chang (葛蘭).
He pioneered an extreme 'slow cinema' aesthetic built on long, static takes, sparse dialogue and durational endurance, with shots that can run many minutes without a cut.
His 2003 film 'Goodbye, Dragon Inn' is an elegy for a real, decaying Taipei movie palace on its final night of operation, screening King Hu's classic 'Dragon Inn' to a near-empty house.
For 'The Wayward Cloud' (2005) he scandalized audiences by blending his musical interludes and pornographic imagery, watermelons doubling as erotic props in a Taipei drought.
After 2013's 'Stray Dogs,' which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, he publicly announced he was retiring from conventional feature filmmaking, exhausted by the commercial cinema system.

He launched the 'Walker' series, in which Lee Kang-sheng, dressed as a red-robed Buddhist monk, walks through cities at an almost impossibly slow pace, including through Hong Kong, Marseille and Taipei.
He moved decisively into the museum and gallery world, exhibiting his slow-cinema works as installations and even mounting shows at venues such as the National Museum and museums in France.
He directed the virtual-reality work 'The Deserted' (2017), an early auteur foray into VR that premiered at the Venice Film Festival's VR competition.
He is openly gay, and themes of repressed and ambiguous queer desire, cruising and isolation pervade his films long before such openness was common in Sinophone cinema.

For years he personally hawked tickets to his own films on the streets and campuses of Taiwan, hand-selling seats because he distrusted conventional distribution and believed cinema-going needed defending.
He bought and renovated an old house in the mountains near Taipei, where he and Lee Kang-sheng have lived and cultivated land, a retreat that informed the rural textures of his later work.
He has repeatedly described his films as being about loneliness and the difficulty of human connection in modern apartment-block cities, a theme he traces to his own solitary temperament.
His film 'What Time Is It There?' (2001) was partly shot in Paris and pays homage to François Truffaut, even featuring an appearance by Jean-Pierre Léaud, the icon of the French New Wave.
He has cited Italian neorealism and the films of Michelangelo Antonioni and Rainer Werner Fassbinder among the formative influences on his austere style.
He frequently casts the same small repertory of actors alongside Lee Kang-sheng, including Yang Kuei-mei (楊貴媚) and Chen Shiang-chyi (陳湘琪), creating a familial troupe across films.
His feature 'Days' (2020), made after his supposed retirement, returned to Berlin and was notable for being almost entirely without dialogue and presented deliberately without subtitles.

He served as a juror at major festivals and his retrospectives have toured institutions worldwide, cementing his status as one of the central figures of the so-called Second New Wave of Taiwanese cinema alongside Edward Yang and Hou Hsiao-hsien.

He has spoken of returning periodically to Malaysia and of his complicated identity as a Malaysian-Chinese who became one of Taiwan's most celebrated directors, never fully belonging to a single nation.

name: Víctor Erice
name_meaning: Víctor comes from the Latin 'victor', meaning 'conqueror' or 'winner.' Erice is a toponymic Basque surname derived from villages of the same name in Navarre, likely originating from the Latin personal name 'Eritius' or the Basque root 'erri' meaning 'village' or 'land.'
intro: Víctor Erice is a legendary Spanish auteur whose achingly poetic, meticulously crafted films explore memory, childhood, and the ghosts of the Spanish Civil War. Despite directing only four solo feature films in fifty years, he remains a titan of cinema.

facts.text: Born in the rural Basque town of Karrantza just months after the end of the Spanish Civil War, Erice grew up in a heavily censored, traumatized society that deeply informed the hushed, elliptical visual language of his later masterpieces.

After relocating to the coastal city of San Sebastián as an infant, Erice experienced his cinematic awakening at age six by watching Roy William Neill’s Sherlock Holmes film The Scarlet Claw at the Kursaal casino, an event he later immortalized in his autobiographical short film La Morte Rouge.

Before fully committing to cinema, he moved to Madrid in 1957 to study Political Science and Law at the University of Madrid, but eventually abandoned those conventional fields to enroll in the Escuela Oficial de Cinematografía (EOC).

He made his professional directorial debut by helming the third segment of the 1969 anthology film Los desafíos, a tense drama starring Dean Selmier that won the Silver Shell at the San Sebastián International Film Festival.

His solo feature debut, The Spirit of the Beehive (1973), was directly inspired by his own childhood memory of watching James Whale’s Frankenstein in a rural village hall, capturing how cinema blurs the line between reality and myth for a child.

For The Spirit of the Beehive, Erice collaborated with cinematographer Luis Cuadrado, who was tragically going blind during the shoot and had to rely on his assistants and his own mathematical understanding of light to expose the film's famous golden, honey-hued images.

The Spirit of the Beehive famously had to sneak its anti-Franco allegories past state censors by adopting a poetic, highly symbolic tone, ultimately becoming the first Spanish film to ever win the Golden Shell at San Sebastián.

His second feature, El Sur (1983), is actually an unfinished film; producer Elías Querejeta abruptly halted the shoot due to budget constraints, forcing Erice to release only the first ninety minutes of his planned three-hour adaptation of Adelaida García Morales’s novella.

Despite El Sur receiving rapturous acclaim at the Cannes Film Festival, Erice felt profoundly betrayed by Querejeta’s financial intervention and has spent decades mourning the unfilmed second half, which was supposed to take place in the sun-drenched landscapes of Andalusia.

For his third feature, The Quince Tree Sun (1992), Erice spent months meticulously documenting hyper-realist painter Antonio López García as the artist attempted to capture the exact autumn light falling on a quince tree in his Madrid courtyard.

During the filming of The Quince Tree Sun, Erice became so obsessed with the passage of time that the documentary literally tracks the physical rotting and falling of the quince fruit, mirroring the aging of the painter himself.

The Quince Tree Sun won the Jury Prize at Cannes and was later voted the greatest film of the 1990s in a massive poll of international cinematheques and festivals conducted by the Cinémathèque Ontario.

In the late 1990s, Erice spent three years writing a massive adaptation of Juan Marsé’s novel El embrujo de Shanghai, only for producer Andrés Vicente Gómez to abruptly cancel Erice’s involvement in 1999 because he deemed the script too uncommercial.

The Shanghai cancellation sparked a bitter, highly public feud in the Spanish press, culminating in Gómez handing the project over to director Fernando Trueba—a betrayal that caused Erice to retreat from feature filmmaking for three decades.

Devastated by the collapse of the project, Erice took the highly unusual step of publishing his unproduced, meticulously researched screenplay as a standalone book titled La promesa de Shanghai to publicly vindicate his artistic vision.

During his thirty-year hiatus from solo feature films, Erice sustained his creative output by directing acclaimed short films for anthology projects, most notably his segment 'Lifeline' in Ten Minutes Older: The Trumpet (2002), which juxtaposed a baby's birth with a ticking clock in 1940s Spain.

After a 31-year absence from feature filmmaking, an 82-year-old Erice secretly shot his fourth movie, Close Your Eyes (2023), in Granada, Almería, and Madrid, reuniting with Ana Torrent, the child star he had discovered fifty years earlier for The Spirit of the Beehive.

The fictional, unfinished film-within-a-film at the center of his 2023 comeback Close Your Eyes is titled The Farewell Gaze, serving as a deeply personal meta-commentary on Erice's own aborted projects like El Sur and El embrujo de Shanghai.

Erice sparked a massive controversy at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival by boycotting the premiere of Close Your Eyes, publishing a scathing open letter in El País accusing festival director Thierry Frémaux of stringing him along and disrespectfully burying his comeback film in the non-competitive Cannes Premiere section.

name: Wes Anderson
name_meaning: Wesley derives from an Old English place-name meaning 'western meadow' (west + lēah, 'clearing/meadow'); Anderson is a patronymic meaning 'son of Andrew,' from the Greek 'Andreas,' meaning 'manly' or 'brave.'
intro: American filmmaker born in Houston in 1969, known for meticulously symmetrical, pastel-hued worlds, ensemble casts, and an idiosyncratic, melancholy whimsy that made 'Wes Anderson' a recognizable adjective.

facts.text: He was born Wesley Wales Anderson on May 1, 1969, in Houston, Texas, the middle of three sons.
His parents' divorce when he was about eight was, in his own words, the most formative event of his childhood, and divorced or absent parents recur throughout his films.
As a boy he made short films on his father's Yashica Super 8 camera, often casting his brothers and pets and building elaborate cardboard sets.
He studied philosophy at the University of Texas at Austin, where he met Owen Wilson when they ended up in the same playwriting class.
Anderson and Owen Wilson briefly shared a cramped apartment in Austin and wrote 'Bottle Rocket' together, first as a 13-minute black-and-white short.
Producer James L. Brooks discovered the 'Bottle Rocket' short after it screened at the 1994 Sundance Film Festival and championed the feature version at Columbia Pictures.
A disastrous test screening of 'Bottle Rocket' in Santa Monica saw audience members walking out, leaving Anderson and Owen Wilson devastated and convinced their careers were over.
Martin Scorsese publicly named 'Bottle Rocket' one of his favorite films of the 1990s, a gesture that helped legitimize the unknown young director.
He is famously a fan of François Truffaut, and his fixation on childhood, melancholy, and precise framing owes much to French New Wave influences.
Anderson has lived for years largely in Paris, and his deep affection for European hotels and trains shaped 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' and 'The Darjeeling Limited.'
His signature symmetrical compositions, centered framing, and whip-pan camera moves are so consistent that 'Wes Anderson' became an internet meme and TikTok aesthetic trend.
He has a long-running collaboration with composer Mark Mothersbaugh of the band Devo, who scored his early films before Alexandre Desplat took over later ones.
Bill Murray has appeared in nearly all of Anderson's films since 'Rushmore,' reportedly handing the young director his personal phone number written on a slip of paper as a sign of total trust.
For 'The Royal Tenenbaums' he used a real New York townhouse on Convent Avenue in Harlem as the family home, dressing it inside and out himself.
For 'Fantastic Mr. Fox' he directed the stop-motion animation remotely, sending detailed video instructions from Paris while the animators worked in London.
He recorded the voices for 'Fantastic Mr. Fox' not in a studio but outdoors on a farm, in attics, and on horseback, wanting the actors to inhabit real spaces.
His film 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' was partly inspired by the writings of the Austrian author Stefan Zweig, whom Anderson cites as a major literary influence.
He shot 'The Darjeeling Limited' aboard a real, custom-painted train that physically traveled across Rajasthan, India, while the actors lived and filmed inside it.
His longtime romantic partner is the Lebanese writer and designer Juman Malouf, with whom he has a daughter named Freya.
He frequently casts the same loyal troupe—including Bill Murray, Owen Wilson, Jason Schwartzman, Tilda Swinton, and Adrien Brody—creating a repertory-company feel across his filmography.
His 2023 film 'Asteroid City' embedded a play-within-a-television-broadcast structure, reflecting his growing fascination with theatrical artifice and the boundaries of storytelling.

name: Wim Wenders
name_meaning: 'Wim' is a Dutch and German short form of 'Wilhelm' (Wim Wenders was born Ernst Wilhelm Wenders), from the Germanic elements 'wil' (will, desire) and 'helm' (helmet, protection), meaning roughly 'resolute protector.' The surname 'Wenders' derives from 'Wender,' related to turning or one who turns.
intro: German New Cinema director born in postwar Düsseldorf, celebrated for road movies, melancholy wanderers and a devotion to American culture; he is also a prolific photographer of empty landscapes and a practising filmmaker into his late seventies.

facts.text: He was born Ernst Wilhelm Wenders on 14 August 1945 in Düsseldorf, just months after the end of World War II, into the rubble of a defeated Germany.
His father Heinrich was a surgeon, and the young Wenders initially enrolled to study medicine and then philosophy before abandoning both.
As a teenager he was an obsessive painter and even moved to Paris in 1966 to become a painter, failing the entrance exam to the IDHEC film school there.
While broke in Paris he survived by spending afternoons in the Cinémathèque Française, sometimes watching up to five films a day, an immersion that converted him from painter to filmmaker.
He worked briefly as an engraver in the Paris atelier of American Pop artist Johnny Friedlaender before returning to Germany.
He studied at the Hochschule für Fernsehen und Film München (HFF Munich) from 1967 to 1970, part of the founding generation of that film school.
He wrote film criticism for Filmkritik and the Süddeutsche Zeitung, reviewing records and movies, and his early passion for American rock and roll permeates his entire body of work.
In 1971 he co-founded the Filmverlag der Autoren in Munich with Rainer Werner Fassbinder and other young directors as a collective to produce and distribute their own films.

His love of America was so intense that his films obsessively feature Polaroids, jukeboxes, diners, and the open road, an aesthetic he later described as 'the colonization of the German subconscious by America.'
He adapted Peter Handke's novella into 'The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick' (1972), beginning a lifelong creative partnership with the Austrian writer Peter Handke.
For 'Kings of the Road' (1976) he shot the film largely without a finished script, writing scenes the night before along the East-West German border in a genuine improvised journey.
His 1984 film 'Paris, Texas,' written with Sam Shepard, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and featured Ry Cooder's haunting slide-guitar score.
Harry Dean Stanton, who starred in 'Paris, Texas,' said Wenders gave him the only true leading role of his career after decades of bit parts.
His American dream collapsed during the troubled production of 'Hammett' (1982) for Francis Ford Coppola's Zoetrope, a film that took years and was largely reshot, souring him on Hollywood.
He documented his own bitter struggle with Coppola and the studio system in the autobiographical film 'The State of Things' (1982), which then won the Golden Lion at Venice.
For 'Wings of Desire' (1987) he again worked with Peter Handke, who supplied the angels' poetic monologues, and shot a divided Berlin in luminous black and white that turned to colour.
The aged storyteller in 'Wings of Desire' was played by Curt Bois, a Jewish actor who had fled Nazi Germany, and the film is dedicated to filmmakers including Yasujirō Ozu and François Truffaut.
He revered the Japanese director Yasujirō Ozu so deeply that he travelled to Tokyo and made the documentary 'Tokyo-Ga' (1985), searching for the vanished world of Ozu's films.
For 'Until the End of the World' (1991) he shot in fifteen cities across four continents, and his original director's cut runs nearly five hours.
He filmed Cuban musicians for 'Buena Vista Social Club' (1999), a documentary nominated for an Academy Award that revived the careers of elderly performers like Ibrahim Ferrer and Compay Segundo.

He is a serious large-format photographer whose images of desolate landscapes in the American West, Armenia, and Australia have been exhibited in major museums and collected in books like 'Written in the West.'
He made the 3D documentary 'Pina' (2011) about the choreographer Pina Bausch, completing it after her sudden death in 2009 and dedicating it to her memory.
'Pina' earned him an Academy Award nomination, and his documentary 'The Salt of the Earth' (2014) about photographer Sebastião Salgado earned another, plus a Cannes prize.
He is a devout Protestant Christian and has spoken openly about his faith, an unusual stance among auteur filmmakers, and once cited the importance of spiritual searching in his road movies.
In 2015 he received an honorary Golden Bear for lifetime achievement at the Berlin International Film Festival, in his home country.
He served multiple terms as President of the European Film Academy, championing pan-European cinema from his base in Berlin.
His 2023 film 'Perfect Days,' shot in Tokyo about a public-toilet cleaner played by Kōji Yakusho, returned him to Japan and the spirit of Ozu and won Yakusho the Best Actor prize at Cannes.
He married five times, with his wives including the German actress and singer Ronee Blakley and, since 1993, the photographer Donata Wenders, who frequently collaborates on his projects.

He once said his films are essentially about looking and seeing rather than telling stories, and he has long preferred shooting on real locations over studios, treating landscape itself as a character.
A passionate music devotee, he directed concert footage and videos for U2, and the band's collaboration with him reflects his belief that the right song can carry an entire scene.

name: Xavier Dolan
name_meaning: 'Xavier' derives from the Basque place-name Etxeberria ('the new house'), borne by Saint Francis Xavier; 'Dolan' is an Anglicized Irish surname from Ó Dúbhláin, meaning 'descendant of Dúbhlán' ('black defiance' or 'challenge').
intro: Québécois prodigy who directed his debut feature at 19, Xavier Dolan became a Cannes darling celebrated for vivid, emotionally fevered films about mothers, queer longing, and youth, while also acting, editing, and designing costumes himself.

facts.text: He was born Xavier Dolan-Tadros in Montréal on March 20, 1989, the son of actor and singer Manuel Tadros, who is of Egyptian Coptic descent, and teacher Geneviève Dolan.

He began acting as a small child, appearing in television commercials, and notably played a sick boy in a series of pharmacy ads that made his face familiar to Québec audiences before he was a teenager.
As a child actor he was dubbed into French films and voiced roles, and he later voiced characters including the young Ron Weasley in the Québec-French dubs of the Harry Potter films.
He wrote the screenplay for his debut 'J'ai tué ma mère' at sixteen, financed it partly with his own savings from child-acting work, and directed it at nineteen, also starring in it and producing it.

That semi-autobiographical debut, about a teenager's volcanic love-hate relationship with his mother, premiered in the Directors' Fortnight at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival and won three prizes, instantly minting him as a prodigy.

He has openly described a fraught, intense relationship with his own mother as the wellspring of his cinema, and mothers — often played by Anne Dorval — recur as the central, mythic figures across his films.
He is openly gay and came out publicly very early in his career, treating queer desire not as a special subject but as the ordinary emotional weather of his films.
He frequently designs or oversees the costumes himself and edits many of his own films, exercising an almost total auteur control that he attributes to impatience and a hyper-specific vision.
He is obsessed with pop music and builds extended, operatic music-video-like sequences into his films, set to tracks ranging from Dalida's 'Bang Bang' to Oasis's 'Wonderwall.'
He directed the music video for Adele's 'Hello' in 2015, shot in rural Québec, and it became one of the fastest videos to reach a billion views on YouTube.
He shot most of 'Mommy' in a square 1:1 aspect ratio, then mid-film has a character physically push the frame wide with his hands in a moment of euphoria, a gesture audiences gasped at in Cannes.

His English-language Hollywood debut 'The Death and Life of John F. Donovan,' starring Kit Harington and Natalie Portman, suffered through reshoots, and an entire performance by Jessica Chastain was cut from the finished film.
He has spoken of his deep admiration for filmmakers like Jane Campion and Wong Kar-wai, and the slow-motion, longing-soaked aesthetic of 'In the Mood for Love' echoes through his style.
He has a long creative partnership with actress Anne Dorval and actor Antoine Olivier Pilon, treating his casts as a recurring troupe across multiple films.

He publicly feuded online with critics and journalists, including a notable spat where he denounced the magazine that gave 'Juste la fin du monde' a brutal review, and is known for his thin-skinned passion about his work.

In 2018 he received the Quebec government's recognition and assorted honours, and he has been a fixture of Québec's star system, his fame in his home province exceeding that of most local politicians.
He turned to television in 2022 with the French-language miniseries 'La nuit où Laurier Gaudreault s'est réveillé,' adapting a play and again excavating buried family trauma.
In 2023 he announced he was stepping back from filmmaking, telling interviewers he had lost his appetite for cinema and was disillusioned with the industry and with audiences' indifference.
He named his production company Sons of Manual after his father Manuel, an unusually filial gesture for a director whose films so often dramatize paternal absence.

He made 'Laurence Anyways,' a nearly three-hour epic about a man's gender transition spanning a decade, when he was barely twenty-two, an audacity of scope that astonished critics at Cannes' Un Certain Regard in 2012.
His films are saturated with rain, slow motion, and sudden bursts of saturated colour, a maximalist romanticism he has defended against accusations of being merely a stylist.
He has said he sees himself first as a writer and storyteller, and writes his screenplays in long, theatrical monologues that pour out of his characters in torrents of feeling.
Despite international acclaim he has remained rooted in Québec and the French language, resisting full assimilation into Hollywood even as Anglophone studios courted him.
By his mid-twenties he had directed five feature films and accumulated multiple Cannes prizes, making him one of the most decorated young auteurs in the festival's history.

name: Yasujirō Ozu
name_meaning: The surname Ozu (小津) combines 小 ('small') and 津 ('harbor' or 'ferry crossing'). The given name Yasujirō (安二郎) combines 安 ('peace, tranquility'), 二 ('two/second'), and 郎 ('son'), marking him as a second son with a name evoking calm.
intro: Japanese director (1903–1963) revered for low-angle, contemplative family dramas like 'Tokyo Story'; a lifelong bachelor, heavy drinker, and meticulous craftsman who died on his sixtieth birthday in Tokyo.

facts.text: He was born on 12 December 1903 in Tokyo's Fukagawa district, the merchant area later devastated by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake.

His father, a fertilizer merchant, sent the family to live in Matsusaka in Mie Prefecture when Ozu was nine, while the father stayed working in Tokyo, so Ozu grew up largely without his father present.
At the Uji-Yamada middle school in Matsusaka he was a poor student and notorious troublemaker who was expelled from his dormitory after writing a love letter to a younger male student.
As a teenager he was so obsessed with cinema that he played hooky from school to watch American films, including those of his idol Rex Ingram, instead of attending classes.
After failing the entrance exams for higher schools, he briefly worked as a substitute teacher in a remote mountain village in Mie Prefecture before his film career began.
He joined the Shochiku Kamata studio in 1923 as an assistant cameraman, reportedly securing the position partly through a family connection and his sheer determination.

He served in the Japanese army in China during the Second Sino-Japanese War, was deployed for nearly two years, and reportedly took part in poison-gas operations, an experience he rarely discussed afterward.

During World War II he was sent to Singapore to make a propaganda film about Indian independence leader Chandra Bose, but spent much of his time watching confiscated American movies, including 'Citizen Kane' and Disney's 'Fantasia.'
He famously filmed almost entirely from a low camera position roughly the height of a person seated on a tatami mat, a 'tatami shot' achieved with special low tripods built to his specifications.
He virtually banned camera movement, dollies, dissolves and fades from his mature work, cutting straight between static compositions in defiance of conventional Hollywood grammar.
He routinely had actors look almost directly into the lens when delivering dialogue, breaking the 180-degree rule that nearly every other director obeyed.
He inserted serene 'pillow shots' of empty corridors, hanging laundry, smokestacks and landscapes between scenes, transitions that became a signature of his contemplative style.
He lived his entire adult life with his mother and never married, famously remarking that making films and getting married were two different things he could not do at once.
He was a heavy drinker who measured his shooting progress in bottles of sake, and his diaries meticulously record his daily consumption of alcohol.

He wrote nearly all his mature screenplays with Kogo Noda, and the two would seclude themselves for months at a mountain inn at Tateshina, drinking enormous quantities of sake while crafting dialogue.
His collaboration with Noda was so intense that the pair claimed they could agree even on the precise placement of a single comma in the script.
He frequently reused the same actors as a kind of repertory family, with Chishu Ryu and Setsuko Hara becoming the iconic faces of his postwar films.
He gave his recurring characters the surname 'Hirayama' and reused names like Shukichi and Noriko across different films, weaving subtle continuities through his body of work.
He was obsessively precise about color, props and set dressing, reportedly repainting objects red to create accents within the frame in his color films.
His debut film 'Sword of Penitence' (1927) is now lost, like many of his early silent works destroyed in wartime and by neglect.
He won the prestigious Kinema Junpo critics' prize multiple times, becoming the first director to win it three years in a row in the early 1930s.
Throughout his career he made over fifty films, yet was long dismissed as 'too Japanese' to export, and his work was barely known in the West during his lifetime.
He admired and was influenced by the American director Ernst Lubitsch and by King Vidor's silent film 'The Crowd,' Western sources for his intimate domestic dramas.
He was made a member of the Japan Art Academy in 1959, the first film director ever to receive that honor.
He smoked and drank heavily and was diagnosed with throat cancer, which he reportedly long concealed from those around him.
He died of cancer on 12 December 1963, his sixtieth birthday, the exact same date on which he had been born.
His gravestone at the Engaku-ji temple in Kamakura bears no name, only the single Zen character 'Mu' (無), meaning 'nothingness' or 'emptiness.'
His international reputation soared posthumously, and critics like Donald Richie championed 'Tokyo Story' until it topped Sight & Sound's directors' poll of the greatest films ever made in 2012.
The German director Wim Wenders made a 1985 documentary, 'Tokyo-Ga,' as a pilgrimage to Ozu's Tokyo, interviewing Chishu Ryu and Ozu's longtime cameraman Yuharu Atsuta.
Ozu kept extensive diaries for decades, and in them he recorded mundane daily details alongside his drinking, providing scholars an unusually intimate record of his private routines.

name: Yorgos Lanthimos
name_meaning: Γιώργος (Yorgos) derives from the Greek Γεώργιος, meaning 'farmer' or 'earth-worker,' from γῆ (gē, 'earth') and ἔργον (ergon, 'work'). Λάνθιμος (Lanthimos) is a Greek surname of less certain etymology.
intro: Greek director from Athens whose deadpan, unsettling films like 'Dogtooth,' 'The Lobster,' 'The Favourite,' and 'Poor Things' made him a leading figure of the so-called Greek Weird Wave.

facts.text: He studied directing for film and television at the Stavrakos Film School in Athens, one of Greece's oldest private cinema academies.
Before features he spent years directing TV commercials in Greece, shooting ads for products and brands, a commercial-craft background he shares with many stylized directors.
In 2004 he was part of the creative team that staged the opening and closing ceremonies of the Athens Summer Olympics, working alongside choreographer Dimitris Papaioannou.

His international breakthrough 'Dogtooth' (2009) won the Prix Un Certain Regard at Cannes and earned a surprise Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film, putting the 'Greek Weird Wave' on the map.
He frequently collaborated with fellow Greek filmmaker Athina Rachel Tsangari, who produced several of his films while he in turn helped produce her work like 'Attenberg.'

His writing partnership with Efthymis Filippou produced the scripts for 'Dogtooth,' 'Alps,' 'The Lobster,' and 'The Killing of a Sacred Deer,' built around their shared taste for flat, affectless dialogue.
'The Favourite' (2018) earned ten Academy Award nominations and won Olivia Colman the Best Actress Oscar, a film notable for being the first Lanthimos feature he did not co-write.
He cites Greek tragedy directly as source material, basing 'The Killing of a Sacred Deer' on the myth of Iphigenia and Agamemnon's bargain with the goddess Artemis.
Emma Stone became his most devoted muse, starring in 'The Favourite,' 'Poor Things,' 'Kinds of Kindness,' and 'Bugonia,' and she also serves as a producer on his projects.

For 'Poor Things' (2023) he built fantastical sets at Origo Studios in Budapest rather than using location work, designing surreal versions of Lisbon, Paris, and a steamship to match the film's dreamlike logic.
'Poor Things' won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival in 2023 and brought Emma Stone her second Best Actress Oscar.
He shot much of 'Poor Things' and 'Kinds of Kindness' with cinematographer Robbie Ryan, and reportedly favours natural light and long, choreographed takes that demand precise blocking from actors.
He shot behind-the-scenes photographs of 'Poor Things' which were exhibited, treating the film sets as material for his own art-photography practice.
His 2024 anthology film 'Kinds of Kindness' marked a reunion with screenwriter Efthymis Filippou and a return to the harsher, more enigmatic register of his Greek-language films.
Jesse Plemons won the Best Actor prize at the 2024 Cannes Film Festival for 'Kinds of Kindness,' in which he played multiple roles across the film's triptych structure.
His 2025 film 'Bugonia,' a remake of the Korean film 'Save the Green Planet!,' again starred Emma Stone, this time having her shave her head for the role.

name: Zhang Yimou
name_meaning: 張藝謀 — the surname 張 (Zhāng) literally means 'to stretch open' (as a bow), one of China's most common surnames; the given name 藝謀 combines 藝 (yì, 'art/craft/skill') and 謀 (móu, 'plan/scheme/strategy'), roughly 'one who schemes/plans through art.'
intro: Zhang Yimou is the most internationally celebrated of China's 'Fifth Generation' directors, a former cotton-mill laborer and acclaimed cinematographer from Xi'an who became China's premier visual stylist and orchestrator of the 2008 Beijing Olympics ceremonies.

facts.text: He was born in Xi'an in 1950 into a family politically stigmatized under Mao because his father had been an officer in Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist army and an uncle had fled to Taiwan.
This 'bad' class background haunted his youth, marking him as suspect during the Cultural Revolution and shaping a lifelong sense of being an outsider striving to prove himself.
During the Cultural Revolution he was sent down to do farm labor in the countryside for three years, then spent seven years as a manual worker at the Number Eight Cotton Textile Mill in Xianyang.
To buy his first camera he reportedly sold his own blood, selling it over a period of months to afford the equipment that let him teach himself photography in the mill years.
When the Beijing Film Academy reopened in 1978 after the Cultural Revolution, Zhang was 27 and over the official age limit, so he was initially rejected.
He appealed his rejection by mailing a portfolio of his photographs directly to the Minister of Culture, Huang Zhen, who intervened to grant him special admission to the cinematography department.
At the Beijing Film Academy he was a classmate of Chen Kaige and Tian Zhuangzhuang, the core of the so-called 'Fifth Generation' of Chinese directors.
His breakthrough came as cinematographer, not director, shooting Chen Kaige's 'Yellow Earth' (1984), whose stark widescreen images of the Loess Plateau announced a new Chinese cinema.
He won a Golden Bear at the 1988 Berlin Film Festival with his very first film as director, 'Red Sorghum,' which also launched the unknown Gong Li to stardom.
He had a passionate, eight-year off-screen relationship with Gong Li that overlapped a remarkable run of films together — 'Ju Dou,' 'Raise the Red Lantern,' 'The Story of Qiu Ju,' and 'To Live.'
His film 'To Live' (1994) won the Grand Prix at Cannes, yet it was banned in mainland China and he was forbidden from attending foreign festivals for a time as punishment.
As an actor he starred in Wu Tianming's 'Old Well' (1987) and won Best Actor at the Tokyo International Film Festival, a rare achievement for a director.
He directed three of his films — 'Ju Dou,' 'Raise the Red Lantern,' and 'Hero' — to Academy Award nominations for Best Foreign Language Film, though he never won the Oscar.
For his arthouse drama 'Not One Less,' he cast real rural schoolchildren and a genuine village teacher as non-professional actors, having them essentially play versions of themselves.
His wuxia epic 'Hero' (2002), starring Jet Li, was a massive commercial hit that topped the U.S. box office and helped open Western markets to Chinese martial-arts cinema.
He was the chief director of both the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2008 Beijing Summer Olympics, mobilizing thousands of synchronized performers in a globally watched spectacle.

The Olympic ceremony became mired in controversy when it emerged that the angelic girl seen singing 'Ode to the Motherland,' Lin Miaoke, was lip-syncing to the recorded voice of another child, Yang Peiyi, deemed less photogenic.
He returned to direct the opening ceremony of the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, making him the first person to helm the ceremonies of both a Summer and a Winter Games.
In 2013 it was revealed he had fathered children in violation of China's one-child policy, and he was fined roughly 7.48 million yuan (about 1.2 million U.S. dollars) by family-planning authorities.

He made his Hollywood directorial debut with the international monster epic 'The Great Wall' (2016) starring Matt Damon, which drew criticism over 'whitewashing' that Zhang publicly pushed back against.

He pioneered large-scale outdoor 'living theater' with his 'Impression' series, including 'Impression Sanjie Liu' staged on the Lijiang River near Yangshuo using a natural backdrop of karst mountains and hundreds of local fishermen.
He also directed live opera, staging a famously lavish production of Puccini's 'Turandot' inside Beijing's Forbidden City in 1998 with conductor Zubin Mehta.
His monochrome ink-painting-inspired film 'Shadow' (2018) deliberately drained nearly all color from the screen, an austere reversal of the saturated reds for which he had become famous.
He has long acknowledged red as his signature obsession — the red sorghum fields, red lanterns, and red wedding sedans recur as a visual through-line across his career.
He served as president of the jury at the 2007 Venice International Film Festival, where he awarded the Golden Lion to Ang Lee's 'Lust, Caution.'
He has remained one of the few Chinese directors able to work successfully both within the state system — directing patriotic and official spectacles — and on the international festival circuit.
His films have repeatedly been censored or temporarily shelved at home, and several of his earlier works carried release bans in mainland China even as they triumphed abroad.
He married former dancer Chen Ting, who is more than thirty years his junior, after his earlier marriage and his long partnership with Gong Li had ended.

Despite directing some of the costliest spectacles in Chinese history, he is known as a relentlessly hands-on, detail-obsessed workaholic who continued releasing films at a rapid pace into his seventies.
